If cosmic rays above 4 EeV exhibit a dipole anisotropy caused by an interstellar magnetic field, the amplitude of this anisotropy would likely increase with energy in a manner that reflects the characteristics of a particular particle population. By comparing this behavior to measurements taken by three experiments, it becomes possible to determine the location and characteristics of distant cosmic ray sources. However, these studies are compromised by the influence of local influences, such as the Galactic center, on the anisotropy. By focusing on the higher energy portion of the available data, it's possible to minimize the impact of these low-energy sources and determine that the anisotropy origin lies at a distance of 12.2 kpc (± 1.3 kpc) from Earth, based on data above 40 EeV, and that there is a charge composition discrimination parameter of 0.025 (± 0.003), indicating that moderate energy cosmic rays are protons. Increasing the analysis to data above 4 EeV results in less precise calculations of 14.0 kpc (± 2.2 kpc) and a charge composition discrimination parameter of 0.011 (± 0.002). All of these findings support the existence of two distinct cosmic ray populations and indicate that the higher energy population contributes significantly to the anisotropy. By comparing this to models of cosmic ray acceleration, it becomes possible to determine the maximum energy to which the sources can accelerate and the minimum energy required to produce the most abundant cosmic ray population. The results indicate that cosmic ray sources can accelerate particles to energies of 50 to 60 EeV and that the most abundant cosmic ray population is primarily made up of particles with energies between 20 to 30 EeV. All of this provides strong evidence for the existence of two distinct cosmic ray populations and confirms that the higher energy population is responsible for the dipole anisotropy above 4 EeV. Furthermore, it determines the location and characteristics of distant cosmic ray sources and the energy at which the most abundant cosmic ray population is primarily made up of protons. All of this adds significant insight to the long-standing debate on the nature of cosmic ray sources and the energy spectrum of cosmic rays. The research faces the challenge of understanding how local influences impact the anisotropy, however, by minimizing their effect, it provides a clear, unobscured view of the characteristics of distant cosmic ray sources. Our research examined the relationship between the centrality of collisions and the variation of the nuclear modification factor (NMUF) in heavy ion physics. We discovered that NMUF varies inversely with centrality, reflecting the interconnected effects of jet suppression and initial state geometry on collision outcomes. This insight leads to a revised interpretation of existing data, allowing for the extraction of charges associated with initial state partonic fluctuations. We further used these charges to develop a new set of variables that characterize partonic fluctuations in heavy ion collisions. These variables demonstrate potential for enhancing our understanding of initial state conditions in such collisions. They may also be useful for making more precise connections between the properties of quark-gluon plasmas studied in heavy ion collisions and the corresponding calculations using perturbative QCD. These calculations consistently predict significant effects of initial state partonic fluctuations on the properties of quark-gluon plasmas, despite previous limitations in measuring the influence of these fluctuations. Our new approach offers a crucial step towards unlocking this essential aspect of QCD. To facilitate further research, we have implemented a numerical method for calculating the charges associated with initial state partonic fluctuations, and we have introduced a new set of variables that can be used to study the properties of quark-gluon plasmas in relation to these fluctuations. We have also leveraged these variables to examine the influences of jet suppression and initial state geometry on collision outcomes, revealing important insights that will prove valuable for interpreting future data. Additionally, we have developed a method for accurately simulating the influences of initial state partonic fluctuations on the properties of quark-gluon plasmas, and we have demonstrated the potential of our approach to enhance our understanding of collision outcomes and the fundamental aspects of QCD. This progress paves the way for breakthroughs in our knowledge of the quark-gluon plasma and its persistent effects on the behaviors of hadrons in medium-sized systems. This represents an important evolution in our research, marking a key step towards unlocking the intricate mechanisms governing the interplay between partons and the hot medium in such collisions. This evolution is anticipated to pave the way for a fresh era in the study of QCD, characterized by a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between hadrons, their interactions with their surroundings, and the fundamental aspects of the quark-gluon plasma itself. This new perspective, rooted in the collective properties of quarks and gluons within medium-sized systems, will, in turn, pave the way for more precise connections between theoretical calculations and observational data.

The success of cancer immunotherapy depends on understanding the interaction between
tumor cells and the lymphatic system, including the influence of the tumor microenvironment.
Quantitative analysis of the lymphocytic infiltration within tumors can be studied using
digitized tissue sections, aided by artificial intelligence and computational biology.
However, there is a lack of standardization in evaluating the spatial distribution of
lymphocyte clusters, leading to disparate results across different studies.
In this study, a novel method is introduced to generate digitized lymphocyte clusters
from tissue sections, inspired by methods used in astrophysics to identify galaxy clusters.
The proposed approach involves three key steps: pre-processing the digitized data,
identifying clusters at different spatial scales, and evaluating the cluster properties
within each sample tumor section, such as density and distribution.
The introduced methods are applied to analyze lymphocyte clusters in tissue sections
from the MSI dataset, showing that tumor infiltrating lymphocytes exhibit a power law
distribution in density, and cluster properties are influenced by the spatial scale
used, particularly in the 2 mm range.
The analysis of lymphocyte clusters from multiple tumor sections reveals that there
is a distinct threshold for cluster density, beyond which they start to overlap,
as well as a relationship between density and distribution at this threshold.
By implementing this astrophysics-inspired approach, a deeper understanding is
gained of the complex lymphocyte cluster structure in tumors, including their size,
shape and spatial distribution, which can provide valuable insights to support
cancer immunotherapy. Furthermore, this method is versatile and can be applied to
analyze lymphocyte clusters in tissue sections from various other cancer types.

Time-series forecasts often require large models that incur significant inference costs, leading some to explore efficient deep learning models such as temporal convolutional networks. We delved into improving TCNs by implementing an automatic dilation optimizer, which simultaneously reduces model size and inference latency while maintaining accurate predictions. By leveraging a collaborative mechanism between dilation factors, our optimizer achieves a 7-fold model size compression on average across three real-world datasets and significantly shortens inference latency by approximately 1.3 times. Moreover, our compressed model performs at a 0.88 AIC score, which is comparable to the baseline TCN model. We also found that our optimizer's success can be further understood through the perspective of predicting time-series components, and it complements other compression techniques like weight pruning. We publicly share our compressed models and the dilation optimizer code to facilitate future research on this topic. Additionally, we introduce a public dataset consisting of forecast data among other resources, which is available upon request. We hope this contributes to the advancement of deep learning techniques for time-series forecasting. Consequently, this dimension criterion ultimately determines the algebra's solvability, as an unsolvable Zinbiel algebra must have a dimension of three or more. Furthermore, with the introduction of the Jacobson radical, we successfully classify all finite-dimensional solvable Zinbiel algebras, demonstrating them to be isomorphic to nilpotent algebras derived from upper triangular matrices. Additionally, the classification of the finite-dimensional unsolvable Zinbiel algebras, first discovered by Burde and Schagler, is expanded to encompass all possible dimensions, with specific examples provided for a two-dimensional algebra discovered previously. Alongside this classification, the previous proof that it is impossible to construct a finite-dimensional solvable Zinbiel algebra with a dimension of two or more is also confirmed. Lastly, the discussion is extended to analyze the properties of the Jacobson radical in relation to the dimension of these Zinbiel algebras. To facilitate the analysis of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, a simple but effective Lie algebra derivation is introduced and leveraged to our benefit. This study's ultimate outcome is a comprehensive classification of the finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, encompassing both solvable and unsolvable types, along with the examination of their geometric properties. This paper examines the relationship between the quark-gluon plasma's macroscopic properties and the microscale, specifically flow fluctuations, which can be measured in heavy-ion collisions. We calculate the ratio of elliptic flow to initial anisotropy for particles of varying charges and find that it remains consistent across different collision energies. Furthermore, we observe that the ratio of higher-order flow to initial anisotropy is influenced by the temperature of the medium, and can be interpreted in terms of the early stages of heavy-ion collisions. Our research also indicates that the ratio of flow to initial anisotropy is resistant to variations in the parametrization of initial conditions. Ultimately, we suggest that studying flow fluctuations can provide valuable insights into the quark-gluon plasma's microscale behavior. Additionally, we introduce a new observable that can help disentangle fluctuations in the initial state from fluctuations in the response of the medium. This observable is expressed in terms of flow fluctuations and initial anisotropy fluctuations, and can be computed using data from current and future experiments. Leveraging this new observable, we anticipate that future experiments will be able to distinguish between the effects of initial conditions and medium properties on flow fluctuations. Consequently, this may pave the way for a deeper understanding of the quark-gluon plasma's microscale behavior. Our novel algorithm ALBA is designed to find first-order counterparts for (D)LE-inductive formulas, particularly focusing on the subset of (D)LE-inductive formulas with bounded quantifier depth. By leveraging the properties of ALBA, we can establish that it has an exponential complexity in terms of quantifier depth and linear complexity in terms of the size of the formula. Furthermore, we demonstrate that by integrating ALBA with the Knaster-Tarski method, it leads to an efficient computation of first-order correspondents for the underlying (D)LE-inductive formulas with bounded quantifier depth. Additionally, we show that by expanding the scope of (D)LE-inductive formulas without a limitation on quantifier depth, the algorithm falls under the category of least fixpoint operations over finite partial orders. Our novel algebraic approach can be applied to a wide range of metabolic networking applications, including the computation of first-order counterparts for inductive logic based fuzzy descriptions of metabolic networks. It is noteworthy that the effectiveness of ALBA is attributed to its ability to simplify the complex definition of (D)LE-inductive formulas, thereby making the code more readable and easier to maintain. Moreover, our research paves the way for various extensions, including the incorporation of additional operators and systems beyond inductive definitions. As a testament to its utility, our algorithm has been successfully integrated into the MetaHOrizon platform, a web-based tool utilized for the analysis of metabolic networking applications. We introduce the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel extension of the Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates model. TV-PARX handles complex phenomena in time series, such as nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks, utilizing a parameter-driven approach. A method for estimating TV-PARX parameters is derived from the expectation-maximization algorithm. We also establish conditions for the consistency of these estimates. Furthermore, we investigate the predictive performance of TV-PARX by conducting simulations and comparing it to alternative models. Additionally, we apply TV-PARX to real-world count time series datasets, obtaining promising results. The TV-PARX framework is versatile, enabling potential adaptations for extending other nonlinear models to handle count data. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields, a novel framework that uses a learning-based state representation to execute complex tasks from brief demonstration videos. By extending traditional kinematics to a motion-based state representation called Neural Descriptor Fields, we can convert demonstration data into task specifications and optimize a controller to reproduce the desired behavioral states. Unlike traditional state-based control methods, our Neural Descriptor Fields controller can be guided by a state representation that is both compact and highly expressive, allowing it to succeed with as few as five demonstrations. We demonstrate the versatility of our framework by successfully completing three distinct tasks: manipulating a flexible rod, placing a disk on top of a pile, and inserting a rod into a slot. We show that our neural state representation can also be adapted to a different robot platform with different kinematic properties. A newly identified red giant anaolog from the high-metallicity globular cluster Tononzintla 2 has been discovered with exceptional chemical properties. This finding, resulting from the CADES spectrographic analysis, reveals a level of abundance in Tononzintla 2 that surpasses the typical metal content found in the cluster's members. The unique chemical profile of Tononzintla 2's new member, which exhibits a rich mix of elements, is uncommon in galactic clusters. A comparison shows that the levels of oxygen, magnesium, and silicon in this red giant are higher than typical observed in the cluster, which is consistent with the trend of increasing abundance of these elements seen in other metal-rich cluster such as M22. Notably, the levels of oxygen, magnesium, and silicon in Tononzintla 2 are more similar to those found in the metal-poor cluster (Ruprecht 106) and the dwarf galaxy (IC 4499), which is notable as it suggests a greater degree of chemical mixing in the metal-rich cluster Tononzintla 2. Additionally, the CADES analysis suggests a higher degree of chemical variation among the members of Tononzintla 2, which is remarkable for a metal-rich cluster, citing examples such as the large difference in oxygen levels between its new member and the cluster's most metal-rich giant. Unlike conventional atomic orbitals, eCPNN representations exhibit higher dimensionality, yet can be accurately projected onto the original angular part via a technique called angular resolution. We demonstrate that these eCPNN representations preserve key atomic properties, such as total angular momentum and electron number, and offer a precise description of electronic spatial correlations. We also show that eCPNNs can be employed to develop a new type of neural network-based atomic neural network descriptor, training it to minimize the difference between its output representations and the training targets, which are typically obtained from highly accurate configuration interaction quantum mechanics. Multiple variants of this trainer have been developed and evaluated, revealing that it achieves remarkably accurate results when compared to costly atomic quantum mechanics calculations. Complex real-world scenes pose significant challenges for 3D object pose estimation, which can be addressed by incorporating projection grouping as a preprocessing step. We propose a self-supervised learning framework, referred to as 3D pose estimation via projection grouping (PPG), which leverages mid-level visual descriptors and geometric transformations to effectively reduce candidates for 3D object pose estimation. PPG incorporates a projection grouping component that uses neural networks to produce candidates for 3D object pose estimation and ensures consistency with image projections. Our framework offers several advantages, including the ability to estimate multiple object poses and adapt to various 3D model categories with minimal training data. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, and our code is openly available for reference.

The peridynamic model's success in predicting materials cracks relies on its micro-mechanics foundation, which suggests that connections between material points can be represented by kinks in the potential function. Researchers have explored various kink structures, including linear, quadratic, and circular forms. In this paper, we introduce a new class of kink models based on the Minkowski question mark function, which includes all previously considered structures as special cases. We demonstrate that this family of models encompasses all non-convex kink functions, and thus, any peridynamic kernel can be viewed as a member of this family. We also establish that the Minkowski question mark function is the optimal representation of non-convex connections within a material microstructure. In particular, we show that for any given kink angle, there exists a non-convex peridynamic kernel with the same rotation and scale invariance properties as its convex counterpart. We further develop the mathematical framework needed to analyze non-convex kink potentials within a material space, and discuss the implications of our findings for modeling materials with complex microstructures. In addition, we introduce the concept of non-convex Kanzaki operators, which provide a direct computational path for evaluating non-convex kink potentials. precision versions of the floating point standard, to evaluate the effectiveness
of four integrator combinations on two significant cases, using the highly
stable alanine dipeptide molecule as our test subject.  Our findings reveal
that the most straightforward method, having the fewest computations per step,
achieves the highest performance but is significantly less accurate than the most
complicated method, which, however, exhibits little difference in computations per

speed and accuracy.  Our research utilizes the AMBER force field and includes
a review of the methods assessed.  Our best-performing option, with the highest

the influence of initial conditions, gravitational perturbations, and other
factors on binary black holes remains an area of ongoing research. The focus of
this paper is on evaluating the impact of starting configurations and energetic

We present a novel algorithm for identifying polymers within medical imaging data.
Currently, polymer detection is typically achieved through probability-based approaches.
Our method treats each monomer as a distinct entity, enabling visualization of the polymer
structure and its spatial distribution within the imaging data. We have developed two key
techniques to do this: first, a multi-object conditional random field infers polymers of varying
lengths by assuming that identified segments contain the same marker; second, a monomer-based
model uses a dataset of reference polymers to inform the inference process. When tested on CT
scans containing gadolinium-based polymers, our results showed that our method outperformed existing
approaches and accurately replicated the complex polymer structures seen in reference images. 
The algorithm's effectiveness also led to significant improvements in contrast agent quantification when
compared to traditional methods. The implementation of this algorithm and training data are
available online. By leveraging this algorithm, healthcare professionals can better analyze imaging
data, which may contribute to a greater understanding of how contrast agents behave in the body over
time. Furthermore, this algorithm has the potential to be applied to other types of imaging and

Real-time formation evaluation is crucial in oil and gas exploration and production, enabling fast and cost-effective decision-making during well operations. Due to the slow transfer of data from the well to the surface, real-time applications must prioritize fast performance. We have developed a method, called LM-EnRML, which employs a restricted matrix formulation for the ensemble neural network to accelerate formation evaluation. This approach significantly reduces the computational time and memory usage compared to the ensemble method, while maintaining precise accuracy. We demonstrated LM-EnRML's effectiveness by applying it to a comprehensive dataset of 24,000 well logs and incorporating various transfer functions, resulting in a 2.5 times increase in computational speed and a 2 times increase in memory efficiency. Furthermore, our method exhibited a 30% reduction in mean absolute error compared to the ensemble technique. LM-EnRML has the potential to revolutionize real-time formation evaluation using neural networks by making it faster, more efficient, and more accurate. Additionally, this approach can be adapted for other applications involving large matrix operations. We have also introduced an open-source implementation of LM-EnRML to facilitate its use across the oil and gas industry. Advancements in deep learning and computing power, coupled with increasing data availability, will continue to propel further enhancements and broader adoption of this technique. Ultimately, LM-EnRML marks a significant step towards increased speed and accuracy in real-time formation evaluation and can serve as a model for solving other complex problems faced by the oil and gas industry. Consider a tropical quartic curve $X_t$ in the tropical rational plane $\mathbb{R}^{2}_{\text{rap}}$, along with a tropical hyperplane $H_t$ of degree $4$ that intersects $X_t$ in exactly $24$ points. It has been shown that there exists a one-to-one correspondence between the rational edges of the complexification of $X_t$ and a certain subset of the edges of the complexification of $H_t$. Furthermore, this correspondence respects the structure of the twisting of edges as they complexify. As a result, we derive that the rational components of the classical complexification of $X_t$ are in one-to-one correspondence with specific components of the classical complexification of $H_t$. Consequently, we demonstrate that the rationality of the classical complexification of $X_t$ is equivalent to the rationality of the classical complexification of $H_t$. Finally, we establish that the latter is not rational. Unlike the case of tropical quartic curves, the structure of twisting edges plays a crucial role in this result. Additionally, we observe that certain classical components of $X_t$ have boundaries that twist in different ways, implying that these components cannot be rational. As a result, we are able to offer a new proof that certain algebraic curves are non-rational, and we present various examples of non-rational classical components of tropical quartic curves. Lastly, we discuss the connection between the structure of twisting edges and the rationality of bitangents in these curves.

To accurately calculate the energy loss function of tantalum oxide, a complex system involving spin-orbit coupling and local field effects must be accounted for. This requires the use of an ab initio method that can handle these interactions in a cluster model. A technique detailed in this paper utilizes the dyson-bottleneck approach within the random phase approximation and local density approximation together with a cluster model that considers local field effects and spin-orbit coupling. This method has previously been successful in modeling the dielectric function of organometallic compounds. Now, it is applied to tantalum oxide, which has a cluster structure consisting of five tantalum and fifteen oxygen atoms. These calculations demonstrate that local field effects are crucial for an accurate calculation of the energy loss function, a finding that is validated through experimental measurement using spectroscopic low energy demonstration spectroscopy. This ab initio method is an effective tool for understanding the electromagnetic properties of complex systems with a cluster structure. This approach could also be applied to other materials with similar structural characteristics. Furthermore, it provides a new perspective on the dyson-bottleneck approach and highlights its potential use in designing cluster compounds with unique electromagnetic properties. This study of tantalum oxide serves as a starting point for a broader examination of the electromagnetic properties of transition metal oxides and organometallic compounds. This phenomenon allows misinformation to spread more easily and persist for longer periods. A significant restriction of conventional machine learning approaches lies in their need for significant computational resources or extensive annotation, limiting their potential for real-world applications. In response, researchers have been exploring new directions that enable complex tasks to be performed with minimal computation or labeling. This study investigates the potential of using simple tasks to learn general task knowledge without explicit training. By leveraging the underlying connections between tasks in a multi-task setting, we can derive a method that learns task-agnostic knowledge from a subset of low-level tasks. This knowledge can then be applied to tackle more complex tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through NLP examples involving sentence classifications and conversations. Our results show that this method successfully learns general task knowledge and achieves notable performance improvements with minimal additional training. Furthermore, we observed successful knowledge transfer to tasks with minimal lexical overlap. This work suggests an intriguing possibility of using low-level tasks as a means to learn general task knowledge in multi-task learning settings. We investigate the complex interactions behind speech generated during teaching by observing how learners semantically enrich their speech when given various instructions and faced with task difficulties. In a experimental setup, we have individuals learn a series of action-based subtasks through either verbal instructions delivered audially or through visual demonstrations. Our findings reveal that difficulty in subtasks and the type of demonstrations given have a significant impact on the concepts expressed by learners in their speech. However, our results also indicate that errors committed during the learning process have a less notable effect on concept expression. Furthermore, we discovered that speech generated under different instruction conditions reflects both the concepts related to the subtask itself and any additional instructions given, even when those concepts are not necessary for completing the task at hand. To model and predict speech development over time, we propose a learning framework that incorporates multiple sources of data and varying degrees of conceptual complexity. Through both analytical and simulation-based approaches, we demonstrate the value of this framework in modeling concept evolution and also explore potential avenues for future enhancements. Additionally, we explore potential applications for this framework in designing more effective learning instructions and improving existing speech synthesis technology. With this research, we lay the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the underlying cognitive processes that shape the speech generated during teaching and learning in a collaborative learning environment. This knowledge can be used to both better predict the evolution of speech over time and to develop more effective learning instructions that also consider conceptual complexity. This research also provides a foundation for a deeper analysis of the underlying cognitive processes and could contribute to the development of more effective learning instructions and speech synthesis technology. These notes describe how certain classical geometric optimization problems can be solved with the help of Euler-Arnold equations, a family of second-order parabolic equations used in quantum field theory to minimize surface area subject to constraint. This surface area issue arises in the context of  quantized non-linear sigma models, and the associated Euler-Arnold equations are a set of second-order parabolic equations, known for their relationship to the Hamilton-Pade equations. We also explore the role of these equations in determining the geometric properties of optimal surfaces. The examples considered include minimal surfaces, willmore surfaces, and soliton surfaces, and we examine how the associated Euler-Arnold equations can be derived from the general case. The surface area issue is typically formulated as a time-dependent problem, however we show that the geometric properties of optimal surfaces can also be determined using the associated Euler-Arnold equations for the static case. This is demonstrated through the analysis of a non-compact example. The notes conclude by discussing possible configurations of optimal surfaces with non-compact boundary in the static case. The possible cases include the inclusion of closed loops, and the scenario in which surfaces have non-compact boundary and contain a finite area of minimal surfaces. The notes also propose several open problems related to the optimal surface area issue. The proposed problems involve the investigation of the geometric properties of optimal surfaces, and the analysis of the associated Euler-Arnold equations for the inclusion of a potential term. The notes also outline the relationship between the optimal surface area issue and other mathematical problems, including the willmore flow, soliton surfaces, and the inclusion of magnetic field. Conversational systems like virtual assistants and customer support bots are becoming ubiquitous, and their quality relies heavily on effective automated testing frameworks. While traditional testing frameworks excel in isolation, they struggle to account for the unique interactions in conversational systems. This paper argues that current testing frameworks for conversational systems are inadequate and need a paradigm shift. It introduces a novel blueprints-based testing framework, which treats each system as a component of a larger interaction network. This approach defines clear responsibilities for system modules and specifies acceptable interaction inputs. By incorporating a formal language and validation tools, this framework can automatically detect inconsistencies in tested code and system specifications, facilitating more effective and efficient testing. This methodology is demonstrated through the development of a working smart home assistant. The evaluation of this system reveals several key findings, including the reduction of errors and the elimination of redundant test cases. Furthermore, this approach can be applied to any conversational system tailored using a similar blueprints-based design. This research offers a fresh perspective on testing conversational systems and provides a versatile solution for this enduring challenge. This methodology is made publicly accessible to inspire further development and improvement of testing methodologies for conversational systems. By leveraging monolingual data within a similar language, the retriever enables the system to access a broader range of past translations. Recent research by Fiori, Lauro, and Anthoniolesi has offered fresh insights into the relationship between natural formulations featuring exotic cones and their corresponding extended formulations. Our study builds upon their findings by conducting a comprehensive analysis of various exotic cones including their extended formulations, with specific focus on the complexities of both forms. Our results reveal that both the natural and extended formulations possess no more than NP-complexity, and further demonstrate that several problems can be resolved through straightforward applications of exotic cones, offering potential implications for future computational biology projects. Additionally, our research raises thought-provoking questions regarding the potential exponential growth of complexities of natural formulations compared to their equivalent extended formulations, as well as the broader concepts of "natural" formulations and their relationships to both computational biology and mathematical theory. Our study is comprised of two main parts, addressing general-exotic formulations and specific-case studies of set partitioning, tree decomposition, and graph decomposition. Our results are accompanied by discussions of both practical and theoretical nature. Lastly, our research is complemented by a proposal for a new graph homomorphism problem, based on the exotic $2$-cone representation, along with a proposed lower complex class for this problem, offering a potential future research direction. Our study is aimed at providing a framework for further research, with potential to offer a graph homomorphism-based solution to computational biology challenges. This study is part of the author's PhD thesis, conducted under the supervision of Michelangelo Lauro.

A common challenge encountered by medical AI models is limited diversity in their training datasets. This study investigates how AI models for MRI analysis behave when trained on diverse datasets. Our experiment involves training and evaluating a model for identifying cardiac abnormalities using MRI data from the OuluMRI dataset. The results show that when trained on a diverse dataset, the model's performance varies significantly, but surprisingly, this performance does not necessarily translate to better results when evaluated on unrelated data. In fact, our findings indicate that the best performance is achieved by models trained on diverse datasets that share similar characteristics. Moreover, we discovered that models can exhibit inconsistent performance even when trained on diverse datasets with similar characteristics, and that there is no clear correlation between performance and data diversity. Lastly, our study reveals that models can perform well on unrelated data when trained on diverse datasets with similar characteristics, and that there is no clear benefit to combining diverse datasets if the model can effectively utilize the data on its own. These findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of AI models for MRI analysis and have significant implications for future studies in this field. Moreover, our experiment paves the way for conducting multi-task training experiments with these models. In addition, our study introduces a new framework for analyzing the behavior of AI models in the presence of diverse datasets. This framework is applicable to other AI model datasets as well. This research is particularly relevant to the medical field where there is a widespread use of multi-center datasets for training and testing AI models. Instead, it focuses on occasional write batches to maximize throughput. In testing, NOVA-relaxed NVMM showed significant performance gains for small, frequent writes and large file operations, with results indicating an average 5-10x performance increase for small writes and up to 70x for larger operations. Furthermore, the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system achieved a 2-3x performance improvement in various Linux system workloads, including PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Linux ext4, and survived for months without memory cell reset in real-world deployments. In addition, NOVA-relaxed NVMM includes several optimizations that boost its reliability, including improved find algorithms and caching strategies, and has the added benefit of enhancing NVRAM's data integrity by reducing write operations. In order to facilitate durability research, the NOVA-relaxed NVMM file system and testbed are open-sourced and available for public use. The Motivation Dynamics framework has been successfully applied in various contexts, and our work offers a new version of the model for systems with multiple agents. By adding a social psychology-based preference function, we can now explore more complex behaviors, including agents meeting up without a leader. We enhance the model by incorporating a state transition function and preference-based selection rule, and then analyze its stability using Lyapunov functions. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate that the modified model exhibits the same stable behavior as the single-agent version. Furthermore, we include a multi-agent extension of the model, and through theoretical and numerical analysis, we find that it can produce the same stable behavior found in the single-agent version, except when there are periodic orbits in the single-agent case. Additionally, we find that the multi-agent version can produce new stable behaviors, including the formation of a sinusoidal orbit and the combination of two stable states. Finally, we apply our model to study the behavior of agents in a dual leadership scenario, and we find that it can produce the same stable behavior as the single leadership case, but with a condition that the dual leadership parameter must be less than a certain critical value. Overall, our results contribute to a deeper understanding of rendezvous behaviors in complex systems.

We examined the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ system to investigate the effects of disorder on magnetic properties and the ground state of this material. Gd and Cm have opposing magnetic moments, which could result in intriguing effects in this system. To study this, we analyzed the structural, thermal, and magnetic characteristics of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds through experimental and theoretical investigations of various compositions. Our studies revealed that increasing Cm composition leads to an enhancement of magnetic moment, contrary to the expected decrease, and a transition from ferromagnetism to antiferromagnetism. This transition is associated with Cm composition and lies within the intermediate concentration range. The results were predicted through the average magnetic moment model and further confirmed by tight-binding band structure analysis and Monte Carlo simulations, taking into account the interactions between magnetic ions and the scattering of conduction electrons. These findings provide in-depth insight into the magnetic properties of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ and offer a framework for understanding similar systems involving heavy-electron magnetic compounds. Furthermore, this research shines a light on the crucial role that Cm, with its unique electronic properties, plays in determining the magnetic ground state of these compounds. The results also suggest that Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds can serve as a suitable platform for investigating phase separation and competing magnetic ground states. Ultimately, this research may pave the way for the discovery of novel quantum states of matter within this system. Along with this, we observed a ground state of antiferromagnetic type by inspecting the thermal variation of specific heat under zero field conditions, a phenomenon that has not been reported previously in this family of compounds. This study introduces a new approach called Hierarchical Range Sectoring (HRS) to break down the large sectors in traditional range sectoring protocols, effectively lessening the frequency of hidden terminals in sensor networks. We also develop a reliable and efficient MAC layer protocol based on HRS, which proactively searches for and avoids potential interference when sending data. Through simulations, we evaluate the performance of this HRS MAC layer protocol and find that it not only reduces the hidden terminal problem by almost 50%, but also increases system throughput by nearly 150% and improves average end-to-end delay by almost 70% compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, we analyze the potential cross-talk and demonstrate that HRS successfully minimizes it to a negligible level. To operate these networks efficiently, we propose a new game theoretical approach called HRS Game Theory (HGTS), which enables dynamic time-slots allocation among individual sensor nodes while considering their unique physical characteristics and locations within the network. Simulations of this HGTS protocol reveal that it facilitates an optimal allocation of time-slots by ensuring fair co-operation among sensor nodes, thereby enhancing the performance of HRS MAC protocol. In conclusion, our analysis indicates that the HRS MAC protocol exhibits superior performance under various network configurations and can be optimized for maximum efficiency through the HGTS protocol. However, further research is required to evaluate the performance of this protocol in real-world applications. Additionally, the HGTS approach needs to be explored for potential applications beyond sensor networks. 

This research is significant as it addresses the fundamental challenges faced by sensor networks by introducing a reliable and efficient MAC layer protocol and a game theoretical approach for optimal time-slots allocation. Different object detection methods suit varying practical purposes, and in many cases, real-world applications involve multiple tasks with no explicit connection. To address the lack of relevant object detection methods for certain tasks and to improve the performance of models on these tasks, we propose a framework that efficiently selects and combines object detection methods. This proposed framework is part of a multi-task engineering tool called MonoMAE, and it effectively leverages object detection methods for individual tasks by incorporating a simple yet effective task-detection method based on patch normalization and linear classification. To further enhance the performance of models, MonoMAE also incorporates a method to isolate task-specific features through a simple yet effective technique based on weighted sum calculation. When evaluated on the DUT-O object segmentation dataset using the MS COCO object detection dataset as pre-training data, MonoMAE achieved a benchmark score of 45.84 mAP, representing a 2.4% improvement over previous best known results for the DUT-O dataset. Additionally, when evaluating the method with weakly annotated image data, MonoMAE achieved outstanding performance with a score of 38.58 mAP, surpassing existing leading methods by 11.2%. When testing the method with the PASCAL VOC 12 object detection dataset, MonoMAE also demonstrated superior performance, achieving a benchmark score of 73.2 mAP on the val set with only weak annotations, a score 5.4% higher than the leading existing method. Using Bayesian methods, a novel strategy is presented to select the parameters of copula models, including Gaussian, Pitman-Yule, and hierarchical Pitman-Yule copulas. The hierarchy of the Pitman-Yule copula, which includes the Dirichlet, makes it an attractive choice for modeling multivariate data with a hierarchical structure. However, the parameter estimation process for these models is typically the domain of simulated annealing or non-linear least squares due to the complex hierarchical relationship between their parameters. The proposed Bayesian approach enables simultaneous estimation of the parameters of these models by utilizing Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, which can be applied to both unstructured and hierarchical data sets, thereby providing a more flexible and versatile solution for modeling multivariate dependencies. The performance of this method is evaluated through a range of simulations, accompanied by an empirical study on real world data set comprising financial time series. The developed algorithm results in accurate predictions and informative posterior distributions for the parameters, which can be used to assess the reliability of these estimations and employ them within forecasting models. This research introduces a novel approach to improving the quality of word embeddings in the context of financial texts. We discover that standard embeddings falter when dealing with certain words like opposites, which are often inaccurately viewed as semantically equivalent. This flaw results from the limited nature of the training data, containing both an opposite (e.g. 'buy' and'sell'). To address this, we propose a method to identify and reoptimize embeddings for certain words based on their inherent properties, reducing the risk of mixing antonyms as synonyms. We demonstrate that our approach successfully rectifies the errors in existing embeddings and facilitates enhanced financial text understanding. We also introduce a novel financial dataset and evaluate our approach by conducting comprehensive experiments, highlighting the benefits of our technique in the absence or presence of antonyms for both simple opposites and complex financial concepts. We show that our method yields superior results compared to alternative strategies, showcasing substantial improvements of up to 108% in accuracy. We make our code and dataset available for public access.

This paper explores the long-term fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization in wideband waveforming, assuming a non-cooperative game model. The strategy for each player is determined by allocating bandwidth among the available communications technologies (CTs), and the objective is to find the optimal mixed-strategy profile that minimizes or maximizes the fair-throughput or sum-throughput, subject to technical feasibility constraints. A new variational active-vessel method has been developed to model the Rayleigh--Bénard instability in an extended cylinder filled with fluid under gravity. This approach addresses the difficulties of maintaining nonrotatory flow and distinct inner and outer layers by introducing a potential-flow exterior and a biharmonic interior representation for the poloidal component of the velocity. By projecting the biharmonic representation onto the active region using mapping operators, the variational framework is enabled while preserving the precise solution behavior at boundary transitions. A convergent strategy based on the iterative application of mapping operators ensures the equilibrium state and unstable modes can be found through a descent method. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in modeling the unstable modes of the Rayleigh--Bénard instability. Our proposed interpretation approach tackles the challenge of language ambiguity by assigning multiple meanings to a single expression. This is in line with the structural compositional framework, which breaks down linguistic structure into smaller parts from sound to meaning. By providing evidence from acoustics to semantics, our system offers a novel explanation for why certain expressions possess various interpretations. This is accomplished through a cycle of analysis, which includes a proposal stage where multiple meanings are assigned to a expression based on its parts, a revision stage where less plausible interpretations are ruled out, and a review stage where the resulting interpretations are examined in the context of the entire sentence. This cycle of analysis produces a set of interpretations that can be studied in the context of sentence structure, allowing us to investigate the relationship between language and meaning. By incorporating a learning component that is responsible for the proposal stage, our system demonstrates a level of linguistic knowledge that can be learned from auditory data alone. When applied to a set of sentences with known meanings, our system is able to discover many of the underlying semantic structures that govern its interpretations. These findings demonstrate that the cycle of analysis provides an effective framework for understanding the complex relationship between language and meaning, and that this relationship can be learned from auditory data alone. When combined with a generation component, this cycle also produces novel expressions with unexpected meanings, demonstrating a level of linguistic creativity. Ultimately, this work is a first step towards developing a theoretical model of the compositional nature of language, as well as a framework for investigating the complex relationship between language and meaning in a data-driven way. In multiagent settings, players can learn to skip unadvantageous actions through experience-based learning, but this often occurs at a slow rate due to the frequent exploration required. As a result, agents may become trapped in inferior actions that, in the long run, lead to minimal rewards. We introduce an innovative approach called Counterfactual Regret Limit Approximate Posterior Expanding Dynamic Policy Learning (CFRL-APLEX), which allows agents to speed up the learning process by leveraging two key concepts: counterfactual regret minimization and value function estimation. By reducing the time needed to identify suboptimal actions, our method boosts the efficiency of learning by helping agents discover better alternatives more quickly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CFRL-APLEX through simulations in various environments, including nontransitive preferences and complex games. Our results show that our approach outperforms multiple comparison methods and exhibits robust performance in testing scenarios. We also derive a theoretical convergence guarantee for our algorithm and provide an analysis of its time complexity. By providing an efficient solution to the large action space problem, our study enables the development of future learning algorithms capable of handling a vast number of actions in complex multiagent contexts. A mathematical framework exists that describes how parton distribution functions (PDFs) change under transformations known as DGLAP evolution. This work develops a method to integrate these evolution equations over a specified range, known as the 'evolution operator,' which can be used to connect PDFs at different scales. By employing this operator, we observed that it facilitates fitting PDFs to a set of data simultaneously for various scales, rather than requiring separate parameterizations for each scale. This approach was applied to a comprehensive dataset of deep inelastic scattering experiments, resulting in a consistent description of data at various scales. The study further enabled the examination of kinematic inequalities, providing insights into the asymptotic properties of PDFs. Moreover, it allowed for the investigation of the onset of asymptotic properties within the measured x-range. This work showcases the potential of evolving PDFs to better understand the internal structure of protons and provides a framework for further research in this field.

as the superbosonization formula. This new transformation enables us to
treat the Schwinger-Dyson equations for the Hubbard model with a finite
dynamical chemical potential. To verify the new transformation's validity,

equivalence of this new transformation to the superbosonization formula
by employing a heat kernel expansion. Ultimately, we utilize the new
transformation to solve the Schwinger-Dyson equations for the Hubbard model
at finite chemical potential, and compare our results with those obtained
through the superbosonization formula. This comparison demonstrates that
the two methods yield identical results for the Hubbard model's dynamical

We investigate how the thickness of LaNiO$_3$ layers within superlattices made from LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying thickness affects their thermal relaxation properties. Our findings show that thicker LaNiO$_3$ layers lead to a smaller, less temperature-dependent relaxation component, and this effect becomes more pronounced at higher magnetic fields. This result is connected to the shift from two-dimensional to three-dimensional transport mechanisms in LaNiO$_3$ layers with increasing thickness. Our research demonstrates the importance of careful material pairing in superlattice studies and provides insights into the thermal relaxation phenomena observed in these materials. Furthermore, our study suggests that LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices may be suitable for further investigation in relation to quantum oscillations in thermodynamic properties. Furthermore, it is observed that the ability to recognize mental states is closely linked to the ability to generate coherent and meaningful text, which is surprising given the distinct nature of these tasks. In conclusion, the MindXGame framework provides a valuable tool for assessing the ability of conversational AI systems to understand mental states and suggests there is a need for further research in this area. This paper examines how the average capacity of a wireless system is affected by the behavior of a reflected signal, which experiences both a change in the system's wavelength and a shift in phase due to the movement of an obstacle in the environment. We are considering a system where the system and the obstacle are moving relative to each other, causing time-varying changes in the behavior of the reflected signal. Formulated in a way that is easy to analyze mathematically, we developed an equation to assess the average performance of the system over time, taking into account the movement of the obstacle, the frequency of the system, and how fast the system and the obstacle are moving. We studied how this equation affects the system's performance, both when the system and the obstacle are moving at the same speed and when they are moving at different speeds, especially in scenarios where the system's speed is much higher than the obstacle's speed, which is equivalent to the system experiencing a moving "frozen" environment. To be able to compute the system's performance over time, we derived an closed-form expression for the system's performance as a function of time, which is based on the properties of a specific probability distribution. With this expression, we are able to analyze how the system's performance is affected by the movement of the obstacle, the frequency of the system, and how fast the system and the obstacle are moving. Furthermore, we developed a method to estimate the system's performance with limited knowledge of its behavior over time, using an adaptation of a well-known statistical estimator. We evaluated the effectiveness of this method through simulations, which showed that it can provide a reliable estimate of the system's performance with a relatively small amount of data, even in scenarios where the system and the obstacle are moving at the same speed, and the system's speed is much higher than the obstacle's speed. The derived expression for the system's performance as a function of time can also be applied to a system where multiple obstacles are moving relative to each other and the system, which was demonstrated through simulations with up to four moving obstacles. With this knowledge, we are able to design an efficient adaptive communication protocol that takes into account the time-varying behavior of the reflected signal and the movement of the obstacles, resulting in a significant improvement in the system's performance over time. The system's performance with our protocol was significantly better than a non-adaptive approach, even in scenarios where the system and the obstacles are moving at the same speed, and the system's speed is much higher than the obstacle's speed

We have developed MG-GLAM, a new code using the Tree-PM method for computational N-body simulations. MG-GLAM succeeds N/GARAM, a previous code developed by one of the authors, and builds upon his work to resolve its significant limitations. The code's mesh generation component leverages an advanced algorithm to optimize partitioning, ensuring even particle distribution and reducing cellular irregularities. As a result, MG-GLAM achieves substantial computational speed gains, with a 10-fold performance improvement, and eliminates previously encountered errors. The code's innovative features include a highly efficient gravitational force calculation method and a refined particle evolution algorithm. Through extensive testing, MG-GLAM has demonstrated its capability to run large-scale cosmological simulations seamlessly. Furthermore, the code has been designed with scalability in mind and can take advantage of multiple CPU cores via openMP, making it an adaptable and high-performance tool suitable for a wide range of N-body simulations. The program is now available as an open-source platform on the GitHub website.

This paper introduces the chordal Schramm–Loewener evolution as a continuous surface evolution in the complex plane, closely related to the Schramm–Loewener map. In this study, we examine the diffusion of nearest-neighbor dimers within two specific network configurations: a triadic lattice and a diamond lattice. Both of these geometries exhibit geometric frustration, yet they are free of obstruction. Our goal is to gain insights into the motion of particles in similar environments by analyzing the dimers' movement and dynamics. The triadic lattice is a recent proposal as a potential network structure for space allocation in agents that interact with their environment through explicit placement. In this context, we investigate the dimers' movement within this structure by considering two types of moves: rotation and translation. Our findings show that the asymptotic rates of rotation and translation are equal to $1/d$ where $d$ is the dimension. Interestingly, this result is similar to that found for geometrically frustrated lattices. However, the rates of move can vary significantly when measured instantaneously. Our analysis of the diamond lattice reveals that the asymptotic rates of rotation and translation approach the square root of $1/d$. Notably, this value is similar to that obtained for the triadic lattice. Moreover, our results indicate that the motion in these lattices can be understood through the application of first-in-last-out and last-in-first-out principles. Specifically, in the triadic lattice, rotation and translation involve moving a neighbor from a distant site to a nearby one, resulting in $\sqrt{d}$ distance coverage. In contrast, the diamond lattice allows for $d$ steps at a time due to its structure. Finally, we compare the motion of dimers and particles by considering the same-dimensional lattices. Our analysis indicates that particle movement can be viewed as dimer movement within the same lattice structure. Yet, the rates of move for particles are $1/d$ as opposed to $\sqrt{d}$. This difference highlights the distinct nature of geometric frustration in particles and dimers. Lastly, we provide implications of our findings for space allocation mechanisms that interact with their environment through explicit placement. According to our analysis, triadic lattices can achieve the same performance as paucity lattices, despite being free of obstruction, due to the geometric frustration inherent in its structure. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that understanding the motion of particles in lattices can provide valuable insights into the behavior of systems that interact with their environment through explicit placement. However, the phenomenon of weak shocks transitioning to strong shocks in certain scenarios remains not fully grasped. To gain insights, we studied the behavior of weak shocks in one-dimensional flows of ideal gases with polytropic properties. Our analysis revealed that the transition of weak shocks to strong shocks is influenced by specific parameters such as the specific heat ratio, and it is characterized by a complex interplay between weak shocks and critical points. By applying the method of matched asymptotic expansions, we developed a suitable inner problem solution that describes the behavior of weak shocks in detail. Our findings were validated through numerical solutions to the full nonlinear equations. Our results indicate that the primary mechanism governing the transition of weak shocks to strong shocks involves a nonlinear interaction between weak shocks and critical points, and it is moderated by the gas's specific heat ratio. Our study provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to various types of ideal gases with polytropic properties. Furthermore, our analysis offers a new perspective on the relationship between weak shocks, critical points, and strong shocks, and it is compatible with the entropy condition. To enhance the reliability of driver assistance systems, we propose a novel approach to predicting actions within a predefined time frame (up to 30 seconds) using video data from a vehicle. Our action recognition model, based on a technique called visual flow, successfully identifies 8 actions such as turning, merging, and braking within a class of 13 categories. To train and evaluate this framework, we utilize a specially created dataset consisting of 13 action categories, collected from various German urban streets. This dataset serves as both training and testing material for our approach, comprising 21,000 still images obtained from multiple cameras with varying field-of-views. Our action prediction model exhibits a precision rate of 73.8% when evaluated against the KITTRAC dataset, surpassing previous records. Furthermore, our framework is capable of predicting actions within a time frame of up to 30 seconds by analyzing a sequence of images, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of driving behaviors. Additionally, our approach demonstrates flexibility in class hierarchy modifications, thereby supporting applications requiring the detection of rare actions. To facilitate replication and advancement of our method, we make both our action prediction model and dataset freely accessible via designated repositories. Consequently, this paper's contributions consist of both a novel action prediction model and a highly useful dataset for replicable evaluation methods. The model distinguishes between global afterglow characteristics and individual ribbon properties in relativistic scenarios. Numerical simulations demonstrate its effectiveness in replicating afterglow evolution in both relativistic and non-relativistic contexts. The model also facilitates in-depth analysis of ribbon structures in ultra-relativistic afterglows. Our findings suggested that splitting vertices can lead to more aesthetically pleasing drawings, given the potential for more flexible graph layout. Deep learning models often suffer from classification disorder, particularly when handling large numbers of classes. To mitigate this, post-processing calibration techniques are employed, albeit mostly assessed in balanced classification scenarios. This study investigates the efficacy of score calibration methods in handling multiple classes and examines their interaction with sampling strategies aimed at reducing class imbalance. Experimental results reveal that popular calibration methods can either positively or negatively affect model performance in relation to the degree of class imbalance, and that they may also disrupt the effectiveness of sampling strategies. Ultimately, our findings suggest that reducing the number of classes can enhance the effectiveness of calibration methods in multi-class scenarios. We further found that, in comparison to intricate calibration techniques, straightforward data augmentation can provide a more efficient approach to addressing both classification and multi-class problems. This research provides a more comprehensive understanding of the calibrated models' performance in multi-class contexts and offers concrete guidelines for their application. Experimental validation is carried out on the robust, multi-class dataset named Standford Online Learning, and the developed approach also extends to the scenario with labeled data. Closed-loop control techniques are increasingly utilized in bipedal robots to enhance their mobility, yet their full potential remains unclear due to the limited number of studies focusing on feedback effects. This research investigates the impact of closed-loop feedback on a five-link bipedal robot moving in a walking pattern by simulating various feedback scenarios using rapidControlLab and MatLab simulations. The results show that a small amount of feedback, about 10%, can significantly improve the robot's performance during the gait cycle, but further feedback exceeds its benefits and eventually becomes counterproductive. This finding is consistent with the theory of reference governors and highlights the importance of carefully designing feedback control systems in complex systems like bipedal robots. Furthermore, the results indicate that closed-loop feedback can lead to more stable walking patterns and reduce the energy consumed by the robot during movement. However, more extensive feedback is found to cause oscillations in the knee and ankle joints despite efforts to mitigate them through adjusted gain values and damping filters. The results provide valuable insights into the behavior of closed-loop bipedal robots and can inform the development of more effective feedback control systems in similar robotic platforms. Additionally, the tested feedback schedules can be adapted for use in actual bipedal robot experiments. We demonstrate that adding a total residue map to the power series field over a finite field results in a computational structure whose decidability is equivalent to the decidability of the theory of that finite field. Conversely, we prove that infinitely large fields have a decidable decision procedure for the same structure. Additionally, we show that over complex numbers, the power series field extended with a total residue map is computationally undecidable. We also establish the undecidability of this structure for the p-adic numbers and demonstrate that doing so captures the undecidability of the algebraic part of the p-adic numbers. We base our findings on recent breakthroughs in the decidability of polynomial rings and the discoveries of a non-computable continuous function from the complex numbers to the p-adic numbers. We present an application of our result to the undecidability of a modified version of a system proposed by Schr\"oder. We also include an analysis of how adding other functions to the power series field over a finite field affects its decidability. Finally, we discuss potential directions for further research and extensions of our results. These advancements offer significant insights into the computational properties of power series fields and their ability to model analytic functions through differentiation and residue calculation. This represents an important extension of earlier work on the computability of the complex numbers, where we demonstrated the undecidability of adding a total inverse function to the complex numbers. This paper offers a more comprehensive exploration of this issue, considering various bases and additional functions, which provides a foundation for further research into the computational properties of power series fields. This, in turn, enables the investigation of analytic functions that can be computed in fields of characteristic zero. We propose that such functions constitute a class worth studying in the context of analytic fields and discuss the implications of our decisions for future research in this area. We define a new class of functions, named the $\Delta$-regular functions, which includes the algebraic functions as a subset, and discuss how they can be added to a basis of a power series field while ensuring the preservation of its computational properties. This enables the consideration of bases that allow the computation of values of $\Delta$-regular functions with arguments in the original field, making it possible to extend the realm of computationally feasible functions beyond the $\Delta$-regular functions through the incorporation of bases of polynomial rings over finite fields. Determining the Higgs boson's decay rate into bottom quarks is crucial for Standard Model parameter measurements and potential signatures of new physics. While the full-lifetime measurement remains challenging, studying the Standard Model's tree-level decay of the Higgs to bottom pairs is more feasible and can be accomplished through bottom quark reconstruction in highly energetic final states of top-quark pair production at the LHC. A new analysis by the ATLAS collaboration utilizes 2015-2016 LHC data to set an upper limit on this decay rate and, for the first time, incorporates an explicit detector simulation in this context. By analyzing top-quark pair data at 8 TeV and 13 TeV, as well as proton-proton reference data at 8 TeV, the study establishes a baseline for interpreting signatures of new physics affecting the Higgs-bottom interaction and sets upper limits on this interaction until the 13 TeV threshold at 1 sigma. Open-source software for matrix computations like BLAS and LINPACK have long been considered the de facto standard, widely utilized as performance benchmarks and building blocks for various algorithms. However, modern computer architectures, characterized by multiple processing units and simultaneous processing paths, have made parallel computing the new standard, rendering conventional Open-source solutions inferior in terms of speed. To bridge this gap, we have created high-performance, parallel versions of BLAS and LINPACK by leveraging the Intel's Math Kernel Library (MKL) to serve as a faster replacement for the industry-wide standard, particularly for applications that could benefit from its speed, such as general linear models. Our research involves replacing the established MKL with our in-house BLAS and LINPACK solutions within the R programming environment and assessing the resulting performance impacts for computational matrix operations. Our findings indicate that although our parallel solutions match the MKL's speed for certain operations on multi-core computers, they fall short in other cases, ultimately producing comparable or even inferior speeds when integrated into the R environment due to various complicating factors. Consequently, we recommend against using these parallel solutions directly within the R environment but rather consider their development as a standalone resource available for other applications. As such, further enhancements to our solutions are necessary before they can be employed in a production-ready context. As an open issue, this research invites contributions from other parties to advance these high-performance solutions for parallel computing. As an evaluation of the R environment's capability to leverage high-performance solutions, as well as a contribution to the community by making these solutions available as a starting point for other applications, we have made our solutions openly accessible via the GitHub platform. As the R environment continues to evolve with emerging computer architectures, there is a pressing need for continued exploration of this research to ensure applications requiring parallel matrix operations can take full advantage of modern computer capabilities. As such, this study is positioned to contribute meaningfully to this evolution by providing a comprehensive evaluation of the R environment's capability to utilize high-performance solutions for parallel matrix operations. We develop a theoretical framework that demonstrates the optimal approach to task allocation involves selecting the most challenging task available, and this strategy yields the best results when tasks of varying difficulties are chosen randomly. Our analysis provides the basis for improving existing algorithmic methods and offers insights into the benefits of selecting the hardest task option. We validate the efficacy of our proposed algorithm in simulation environments featuring changing numbers of agents and diverse task difficulty distributions. Furthermore, we showcase the algorithm's applicability to real-world challenges, such as the energy efficiency problems we study in the context of the Intel NUC cloud platform. Our findings highlight the algorithm's ability to achieve superior performance compared to alternative methods and provide a framework for improving existing algorithmic methods. Consequently, it is hoped that this work will inspire a groundswell of interest within the community, leading to further breakthroughs that will be crucial in addressing the complex challenges associated with rare signal identification in high-energy particle collisions. This research focuses on enhancing the privacy protections of vertical federated learning (VFL) through the incorporation of privacy-enhancing technologies. Although existing VFL frameworks have been criticized for vulnerabilities in learning sensitive data without revealing information about the individual contributors, our investigation reveals that these protocols are susceptible to inference and membership attacks. We consequently propose an alternative protocol, leveraging private aggregation methods such as private sum and Euclidean distance, to protect contributors' sensitive information. The proposed solution ensures the privacy of data contributors through the use of private comparison and aggregation techniques, ensuring that only aggregated data is shared without disclosing individual contributions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by developing a convolutional neural network-based model and incorporating the private aggregation of activation functions, thereby protecting sensitive image data while facilitating reliable model training. The proposed framework has several advantages, including support for anonymous data contribution, elimination of trusted parties, and minimal communication overhead. The feasibility of this approach was validated through experiments utilizing publicly available datasets, showcasing its capacity to achieve accurate results while providing robust data protection. The evaluation results revealed that the proposed protocol offers satisfactory privacy guarantees for both low-density and high-density data scenarios. Furthermore, an exploratory analysis into the optimal selection of privacy parameters is also included, along with the benefits of the proposed approach in relation to other protection methods. The implementation of the proposed protocol is made available as an open-source Python framework. The evaluation results are made available in the accompanying dataset, offering a practical framework for implementing VFL applications with enhanced privacy protections. The research is further underscored by theoretical guarantees providing privacy assurance in the form of differential privacy, with the proposed protocol offering improved privacy resilience against various attacks. The findings are expected to facilitate the development of secure VFL applications leveraging sensitive data while ensuring robust privacy protections for contributors. In recent years, Random Fourier Features have gained significant attention as a cost-effective method for mapping data into Hilbert spaces without having access to explicit kernel functions. However, RFFs' reliability depends on their feature dimension and learning rate, which require careful adjustment, thereby limiting their practical application. To address this issue, this paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features, a new approach that significantly reduces the feature dimension required for accurate prediction performance while eliminating the need to adjust the learning rate. The proposed method learns the optimal feature dimension empirically through a simple dimension reduction mechanism and adapts this approach to a Neural Network framework, demonstrating improved performance across multiple classification tasks involving functional data sets and text classification, and further extends this method to regression tasks and gene expression prediction. The results show that PRFFs can efficiently learn optimal feature dimensions, leading to superior prediction performance compared to traditional RFFs and NN baselines. The source codes for the proposed method and experiments are available online at https://github.com/heng3305/PRFF. The paper also introduces the Kernel-PRFF method, an extension of the algorithm for kernels without explicit expressions, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in motor anomaly detection and significantly outperforming the baseline in brain MRI analysis. The proposed method's efficacy is further validated by an analytical method with guaranteed performance and expression-free kernels. The paper's contributions include the pseudo learning method for optimal feature dimensions, the extension of kernel-PRFF to state-of-the-art performance, and the discussion of the algorithm's theoretical guarantees. The paper also introduces the PRFF framework's connection to the Random Fourier Feature technique and explores the method's applicability to Neural Networks. Nevertheless, a significant drawback of this method is the requirement for a vast, well-labeled dataset to ensure generalizability. In contrast, the present study reveals that a cardiac image dataset with diverse and severe abnormalities can serve as a robust foundation for training a network.
