We explored the application of transfer learning to cross-lingual speech recognition. To compare the learning behaviors of our models in languages with high and low similarity, we selected two groups of languages, English and non-English, for the superdomain and four European languages (English, Spanish, French, and German) for the subdomain, respectively. To facilitate reproducibility, we created a multi-lingual speech recognition dataset called EuroDS. This dataset contains 2,197 hours of labeled data and follows a hierarchical structure, allowing for effective transfer learning. Our experiments involved evaluating various transfer learning strategies on EuroDS. The results showed that all our proposed approaches achieved better performance than the non-transfer learning method and a simpler transfer learning technique. Interestingly, the data still played a crucial role in our model evaluations. Additionally, we observed that the performance of models improved more significantly for languages with higher similarity. This led to better results for the low-similarity group than the high-similarity group without additional training data. However, when the similarity between languages increases, the performance improves with more training data but eventually plateaus due to the dominant influence of the data. To further analyze the effects of transfer learning, we conducted a series of experiments under restricted computational resources. These experiments led to several key observations: (1) the performance of all our proposed transfer learning strategies outperformed the non-transfer learning method, (2) the data still played a critical role in our model evaluations, and (3) the performance of models increased more substantially for languages with higher similarity. This prompted us to train a cross-lingual speech recognition model on the entire superdomain dataset. When tested on the subdomain dataset, our model showed a significant performance improvement (13.5%) over the baseline model without cross-lingual training. Moreover, we found that this improvement was more pronounced when the similarity between languages increased. Nonetheless, the difference was not as distinct as the improvement obtained with transfer learning. Ultimately, our experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of transfer learning for cross-lingual speech recognition. To facilitate further research, we have made the EuroDS dataset and all related models available for public access. Additionally, we have released our code based on the PyTorch framework on the GitHub repository https://github.com/speechli-laix/cross_lingual_speech_recognition. Our study reveals that high Gd content leads to an unexpected transition from the pyrochlore to the A2BO3 structure, accompanied by a significant shift in optical direct gap energy. Notably, both pyrochlore and A2BO3 phases exhibit similar bandgap energies, suggesting that the former's electronic properties are influenced by tailored tailoring of the Gd spin states. Our findings demonstrate the potential of GdInO3 to exhibit ferromagnetic semantics with optical properties, making them suitable for spintronic devices that incorporate optical control. Additionally, we observe that increasing Gd concentration results in enhanced ferromagnetic interactions and opposing effects on the spin-lattice relaxation time and magnetic anisotropy. We examine the problem of allocating goods among agents, where agents are matched with items through a one-to-one correspondence denoted as a permutation. A previous proposal by Anshelevich and Dughmi presented the Round-Robin mechanism, which generates a fair allocation for each agent based on their ordered list. Anshelevich and Dughmi established the feasibility of achieving approximately fair outcomes under this method. In this work, we demonstrate that the Round-Robin method can produce fair outcomes with a guarantee of $\frac{1}{k}$ when considering $k$-fairness. Notably, this guarantee can be achieved without relying on additional utility maximization parameters. We also compare the Round-Robin method to the cut-and-choose algorithm, which has a guarantee of $\frac{2}{k}$ for $k$-fairness. Our comparison shows that the fairness of the Round-Robin method exceeds that of the cut-and-choose algorithm for $k$ greater than 2. We illustrate the fairness properties of the Round-Robin method through numerical experiments and analyze its sensitivity to different utility functions. Our findings suggest that the fair allocations generated by the Round-Robin method can be quite extreme in some cases, with one agent obtaining significantly more value than the other agents. Finally, we discuss potential applications of this method in allocating goods to agents based on their performance, such as matching teams with tournament spots or allocating prizes in competitive games. This study revealed a significant correlation between the spectral energy distribution of HII regions and their locations within the galaxy's disk. HII regions situated closer to the galaxy's center tend to have larger effective radii, which can be as large as 3 kpc, whereas those farther from the center have smaller effective radii. By calculating the gravitational potential of UGC 8839, we found that the majority of HII regions lie within the disk's potential, with a smaller number located in the bulge's potential. When comparing our findings to similar HII region populations in other spiral galaxies, we noticed that the HII regions in UGC 8839 are located on average 1 kpc further from the galaxy's center. This distribution suggests a larger disk scale length in UGC 8839, which is consistent with the galaxy's overall stellar disk structure. By modeling the star formation history within UGC 8839, we estimated a star formation rate that is about half of what is typically found in similar spiral galaxies. This reduced star formation rate may be contributing to the larger galactocentric radii of UGC 8839's HII regions. However, we also consider the possibility that the larger disk scale length itself may be the result of a higher specific star formation rate within UGC 8839's disk over the past billion years. Furthermore, we observed a smaller, young stellar population located near the galaxy's center, which may be the result of a minor merger. People confront uncertainty about the causes of poverty, which affects how they view the need for wealth redistribution. This research explores the varying expressions of this uncertainty in a simplified economic model consisting of three segments: those fortunate enough to have opportunities that may be influenced by luck, those whose opportunities are entirely determined by luck and are therefore unchangeable, and those whose fortunes are entirely determined by luck and can be altered by changing opportunities. The aim of this study is to identify which of these groups elicits the strongest public sympathy for redistribution. The results show that when luck has a direct impact on income, it sparks the most significant desire for redistribution, both in a survey of 1,000 individuals and in an experiment involving 1,500 participants. Notably, the data reveal an interesting contrast in behavior. In a scenario where luck affects opportunities indirectly, the public's demand for redistribution is minimal. However, when luck has a direct effect on income, the public's demand for redistribution increases substantially. Furthermore, an experiment involving lotteries reveals that the public's desire to help individuals affected by luck in the second category far exceeds their desire to assist those in the first category. These findings have implications for the perceived fairness of economic systems and may help explain the observed disparity in public charity versus government assistance in many countries. The study also provides evidence for the limited impact of moral sentiments expressed by Joseph Chamoux in relation to economic fairness. Additionally, the results suggest that the strength of charitable moral sentiments is insufficient to counterbalance the stronger desire for justice expressed through support for redistribution. The findings of this research have significant implications for the design of policies aimed at reducing poverty and inequality. The discovery that the public's desire for redistribution is fueled by the perception of injustice sparked by luck's direct impact on income opens up new policy pathways. The study proposes implementing a progressive tax system that targets those whose incomes are most closely tied to luck's direct impact. The results from the survey and the experiment provide the foundation for this policy recommendation. The study also explores the possibility of individuals making more informed decisions about redistribution by providing them with clear information about the luck-based components of individuals' incomes. The discovery that charitable moral sentiments play a limited role in relation to economic fairness challenges Joseph Chamoux's argument. The study suggests that Chamoux's argument applies only to charitable acts, but not to justice-driven expressions of the same moral sentiments. This paper explores the task of inferring high-dimensional structures, specifically hypergraphs, from lower-dimensional structures, namely graphs and their embeddings. We investigate two scenarios: first, reconstructing a hypergraph from a single graph; second, hypergraph reconstruction based on multiple graphs that represent different projections of the same high-dimensional structure. We discuss theoretical limitations as well as possible approaches and examine the feasibility of hypergraph reconstruction through a practical example involving the analysis of a musical composition. We propose a hypergraph reconstruction method that leverages network flow algorithms and demonstrate its applicability to a real-world dataset. Our findings indicate that this approach can effectively recover hypgraph structures from their projections and demonstrate the method's potential for further development. We also introduce a new concept called the'structure profile' of a hypergraph that captures its dimensional characteristics and is viable for comparing similar structures. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for advanced graph analysis tools that can operate across multiple dimensions. The directionality of emission from lasers can be characterized by a divergence angle, which indicates how broadly emitted light spreads. Due to the nature of transverse modes in standard single-mode lasers, their directionality is largely consistent, which is reflected in the narrow divergence angle. In contrast, the directionality of emission can vary significantly in fiber lasers, sometimes being quite broad in one direction but narrow in the other. This phenomenon arises because the propagation of light within these lasers is influenced not just by the fundamental transverse mode but also by higher-order modes that can develop when there are small defects in the laser cavity, notably where the light intensity becomes low in certain directions. As a result, the directionality of emission from these lasers can exhibit an apparent anisotropy. We have observed an even more marked anisotropy in the emission from fiber lasers based on double-clad design, where the broad emission direction aligns with the direction of maximum pump power. We found that this anisotropy can be utilized to select lasers emitting wide-beam or narrow-beam radiation by adjusting the amount of back reflection from the end of the fiber. We have also used a different type of laser based on a single-mode fiber with a integrated microresonator to demonstrate the anisotropy's applicability to the selective emission of wide-beam or narrow-beam radiation. We believe our findings will lead to the development of laser systems capable of wide-beam emission, offering potential for their use in the study of particle interactions with wide-beam light. We also propose the concept of choosing wide-beam emission over narrow-beam emission as a controllable means to prevent particle loss due to the large difference in emission directions. This approach could provide a more clear understanding of particle behavior in wide-beam environments. We have tested our concept with lanthanide-based lasers and have achieved wide-beam emission, and we believe it could be applied to other types of lasers as well. We investigate the scattering of coherent light from atomic ensembles using atomic gases with different temperature characteristics, focusing particularly on the behavior of the two-time second-order correlation function. Initially, we consider a highly coherent atomic state, for which we derive an analytical formula for the correlation function, and demonstrate that it can be manipulated to display various temperature-independent patterns. Furthermore, we develop a simulation to examine the impact of increasing temperature on the correlation function, and observe how it transitions from displaying peaks at time differences of $\Delta t = 0$ to exhibiting a periodic behavior at higher temperatures. Our study also explores how moving from coherent to propagating light affects the correlation function, and reveals that even with temperature-controlled atomic states, the correlation function can exhibit distinct structures, potentially utilising them as 'fingerprint' patterns for the atomic environment in question. Additionally, we analyse the transform of the correlation function in momentum space, and discover that it transitions from displaying peak structure at $\Delta t = 0$ to exhibiting a more intricate pattern with rising temperature. Our research suggests that examining the correlation function in momentum space can provide valuable insights into the atomic system's temperature-dependent behavior. Finally, we propose using the correlation function as a means of controlling the scattering of light from atomic ensembles, and presenting a possible design for an atomic system with desired properties. This could enable the development of novel sources of quantum light, such as below-threshold modes, soliton-like states, and entangled photons. Ultimately, this study aims to lay the groundwork for a deeper understanding of and better control over the scattering of light from atomic ensembles, which is crucial for implementing efficient and controlled quantum light-matter interaction systems. Offline learning for multi-agent systems typically involves training individual agents without any online interaction, which can result in unsatisfactory results due to the lack of inter-agent connections in the data. To address this issue, we introduce the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework, which introduces a novel method for offline learning in multi-agent systems. In this framework, each agent has its own unique trajectory and they share a co-occurring structure, which can be modeled as training agents with shared factors that influence their individual trajectories. We demonstrate that by introducing a linear encoder for the SIT framework, we can effectively utilize offline data and reduce the gap between online and offline performance. Our proposed Baseline-encoder method serves as a starting point for our main contribution, which involves an iterative method for optimizing the encoder that utilizes online observations and has the benefit of being easy to implement with various offline datasets. Our findings, which include results from simple cooperative games and a complex multi-agent classification task, demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing offline learning approaches. The code for our method has been made publicly available.

Deep learning techniques are increasingly used for medical image registration due to their ability to learn complex patterns, thereby providing a more accurate and robust alternative to conventional image processing methods. Despite the benefits, some researchers have raised concerns that deep learning networks can produce biased results when applied to images with varying intensity levels. To address this issue, we propose using a Convolutional Neural Network that processes both image features and a similarity measure, derived from the intensity distribution, to regulate the network's behavior. By incorporating this similarity measure, we enable the network to focus on structural analyses rather than intensity-based processing. The proposed framework shows improved results compared to the baseline CNN in a series of brain MR image registration tests, with results also comparable to atlas-based methods. We also compare our method to state-of-the-art deep learning image registration techniques at various distortion levels. The proposed framework provides a new perspective on medical image registration, focusing on structural analysis rather than intensity-based processing, and we make all code publicly accessible to facilitate further development and application. We investigate current properties at the surface of two types of systems: bosonic optical lattices filled with atoms of the same species, and fermionic lattices filled with two different species of atoms. Our study focuses on systems with strong tunneling, where surface-dwelling particles move freely despite being part of a larger connected network. We develop an efficient theoretical approach by treating the surface as an independent layer with interactions with a continuous electron gas. Our approach allows us to identify robust surface currents that exist across multiple thicknesses of the system, characterized by well-defined minimumpartition widths, and precisely determined lifetimes. We found that in both bosonic and fermionic systems, surface currents can be robust due to tight binding or nearly flat bands at high energy levels. We further found that short-range on-site interactions strengthen these surface currents, while long-range interactions cause them to weaken, and that spin and orbital imbalanced layers can demonstrate robust surface currents at both high and low temperatures, our calculations for the latter using the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wing theorem. We present experimental guidelines for observing these surface currents, involving the measurement of entangled states and current correlations as an electron gas interaction strength. We've modeled the behavior of massive star clusters at high redshifts (>10) to gauge the number of binary black hole mergers caused by the collapse of primordial matter. By analyzing how many of these events are observable, we've calculated the merger rate density of massive star clusters at z = 10 to be approximately 0.06 events per year per gigaparsec cubed. This rate peaks at z ≈ 8 and then declines as cosmological expansion dilutes primordial matter, making it more difficult for binary black holes to merge with matter-induced gravitational waves. To date, all detected binary black hole mergers have been composed of medium to high metal content, so it's unclear whether primordial binary black holes can be identified through such evidence alone. Nevertheless, with the addition of a more sophisticated model of binary evolution, we've found that primordial white dwarf binaries can be distinguished from their heavier counterparts based on their merger rates in gamma-ray bursts. In the case of a binary system consisting of a primordial white dwarf and a heavy companion that generates a gamma-ray burst when it merges, we estimate that this event could be observable up to z = 4 without being masked by other gamma-ray bursts. If produced at the current rate of binary star formations in 30 days of gravitational wave observations, there's a less than 1% chance of missing such an event. These findings highlight the potential for binary black hole mergers caused by primordial matter to be observed through gravitational waves and for white dwarf binaries to be identified through gamma-ray bursts, providing a richer source of multi-messenger signatures of the early universe. These events will not only shed light on the distribution of heavy elements in the early universe but may also offer insights into how binary stars formed at the earliest stages of the universe's existence behaved during their lives. Moreover, they will provide a chance to examine how binary stars are affected by cosmological expansion over billions of years and offer a chance to study binary evolution in extreme conditions that cannot be replicated through computer simulations. To facilitate the identification of these events, we propose developing a detection algorithm that can effectively distinguish these unique events from the regular merger population. Synchronizing such searches with forthcoming generation gravitational wave and gamma-ray burst detectors will significantly enhance the chances of detecting these distinctive binary black hole and white dwarf mergers, making them a promising area for multi-messenger astronomy to gain insight into the early universe's binary star evolution. Both solid-state and optical applications of quantum optics benefit from studying the interplay between single-photon properties and many-body systems. A key component in this interplay are quantum emitters that can interface with system edges, which are inherently protected from scattering and backscattering due to their non-local properties. In this review, we discuss in parallel both theoretical and experimental aspects of defect-based quantum emitters in photonic crystals, focusing specifically on those based on postulated and observed one-dimensional topological phases. We examine the unique properties of these emitters when interacting with photons in both the radiative and non-radiative regimes. We also review the current state of experimental investigations using these emitters, detailing studies that have demonstrated the creation of non-local, entangled states between single photons and edge modes. As research continues to evolve, we expect defect-based quantum emitters to play a key role in the development of applications for one-dimensional topological photons. This package is designed to facilitate the development of new scenarios for experiment-theory comparison. This study explores how connected automation can manage journey planning by analyzing the effects of traffic signals on vehicle trajectories. To illustrate this, a scenario is considered where a connected automated vehicle approaches a four-way intersection, aware that another vehicle will enter the intersection during the red phase. Current connected automation frameworks typically focus on cooperative behavior to avoid collisions, but the role of traffic signals in this process is overlooked. An analysis of the yellow and red phases reveals that traffic signals provide critical information for preventing rear-end collisions and facilitating efficient journey planning. As a result, connected automation systems in urban areas should be designed with a sensing-and-control approach that incorporates impending traffic signals into state estimation and trajectory planning algorithms. To demonstrate this, a sensing-and-control approach is applied to an intersection scenario, and the performance of this method is evaluated against a conventional tracking filter and trajectory planning strategies in simulated and real-world environments. The results show that this approach reduces the risk of rear-end collisions and facilitates faster journey planning. However, it introduces delays caused by sensor data processing, which can be mitigated by incorporating additional safety buffers into the traffic signal design. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a new fastening protocol for text game simulations, which speeds up the process by reducing the number of actions required to solve the game from linear to logarithmic time. We demonstrated TextWorldExpress's effectiveness by applying it to TextWorld and observing a significant increase in simulation throughput of up to 800 times, thanks to a more efficient planning approach that capitalizes on the protocol's properties. We also analyzed various aspects of TextWorld and identified patterns that the protocol facilitates, such as hierarchical structure and conditional dependencies, and explored potential challenges it may face with games that incorporate obstacles and multi-step goals. The text game simulation community can benefit from evaluating their own games using TextWorldExpress and considering our proposed solutions to improve simulation performance. Additionally, we offer TextWorldExpress as a protocol for other text-based games, and encourage discussion on its potential applications and limitations. All implementation details and evaluation results are available for review and feedback. We look forward to contributing TextWorldExpress to the next competition as part of the Integrated Reasoning Competition. We investigate various efficient NLP models with limited training data and minimal preprocessing, focusing on data augmentation as a primary enhancement technique. Despite the potential of GAN-based methods, they are not utilized in our study due to difficulty in training balanced training sets. Instead, five straightforward data augmentation techniques are tested with multiple deep NLP models on three key NLP applications. Our findings reveal that augmenting the training set significantly improves performance across all experiments, with model efficiency also showing a positive correlation with NLP model complexity. However, higher-order efficiency is observed for some models, suggesting certain models can handle limited training data with aid of augmenting. Our work provides NLP researchers with actionable results that can inform future studies on model efficiency, data efficiency, and augmenting techniques. Introducing time-varying pricing in electricity markets encourages short-term optimization, thus potentially reducing the grid's need for late adjustments. Nevertheless, some sectors, like the industrial sector, might not readily adapt to these changes due to existing long-term contracts. As a result, the opportunity exists for the grid operator to take advantage of anticipated price fluctuations in the wholesale market to delay or accelerate power delivery. This delay or acceleration of power delivery can lead to significant benefits for the grid operator, particularly in regions with high retail electricity costs and significant industrial participation in the wholesale market. This paper explores the possibility of creating a separate redispatch market where the grid operator can buy delayed power at a premium and sell accelerated power for a profit. This is set within a theoretical framework that accounts for the behavior of market participants and is mathematically represented through dynamic programming. A simulation based on historical data from the Midwestern United States demonstrates that introducing this market would result in the grid operator procuring time-based redispatch contracts instead of location-based ones, thus requiring a dynamic valuation approach. Furthermore, it is shown that time-based redispatch contracts could be valued through a marginal value approach, and that the opportunity to buy delayed power is subject to diminishing returns. This research provides a theoretical foundation for designing optimal pricing mechanisms in redispatch markets. A key conclusion is that the value of time-based redispatch increases with the duration and exceeds the current location-based redispatch value, thus highlighting the need to shift towards time-based pricing in the wholesale market to fully utilize the grid operator's redispatch opportunities. This research also offers a theoretical foundation for extending the time-based pricing approach to other sectors, such as the residential sector, by taking into consideration the sector's adoption barriers and contractual agreements. Ultimately, this research suggests that introducing time-based pricing in the wholesale market will result in the grid operator procuring time-based redispatch contracts, and that this requires a dynamic valuation approach that reflects the behavior of market participants. This research provides a theoretical foundation for designing optimal pricing mechanisms in redispatch markets and offers a novel valuation approach for time-based redispatch contracts, thus providing valuable insights for policymakers and grid operators. We examine a particular set within the Galois groups of rational function fields in one variable, over a finite field of positive characteristic, and establish an explicit upper bound on the density of elements within this set. This finding is tightly aligned with the polynomial analogue of the famous Bateman-Horn conjecture, and demonstrates that for a specific class of polynomials, the number of solutions to a particular equation exceeds expectations by a significant margin. Notably, this outcome is achieved with no restrictions placed on the degree of the polynomials in question. Prior work by Kummer and Vinberg focused on the case of quadratic polynomials, and this research provides a comprehensive extension of their findings to polynomials of any degree. The devised upper bound is particularly noteworthy as it is presented in a form that is easily compatible with the proposed polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture. To establish this result, an innovative application of a recent theorem by Dietmann and Hayes proved invaluable. This novel result is also shown to have implications for the distribution of Galois groups in certain polynomial extensions, and suggests that the density of a specific subset is in line with the predictions outlined in the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture. To conclude, a particular connection with questions regarding the distribution of Chow-Hassner groups is established, and it is proposed that further research into this topic is warranted. Additionally, this research is seen as a preliminary step towards a comprehensive understanding of the behavior of Galois groups in rational function fields over finite fields of positive characteristic. Lastly, it is suggested that hyperelliptic curves could provide a suitable context in which to study these phenomena in a broader framework. Consequently, this research is seen as a starting point for, rather than a culmination of, ongoing investigations. It is with this in mind that the results presented herein are placed within the context of the proposed polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, and it is the firm belief of the author that further work in this area will provide valuable insights into both the behavior of Galois groups in rational function fields and the distribution of Chow-Hassner groups. It is also hoped that the connection established between these topics and the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture will provide a stimulus for additional research into these areas. The discovery of a polar vortex at the North Pole of Saturn is confirmed through latest observations from the Cassini spacecraft, and it shares many characteristics with the persistent southern vortex at the planet. Although the north vortex disappears each summer, and a circular central stratospheric hot spot appears at the pole during that time, this finding shows the two-vortex configuration at Saturn lasts through the winter and early spring seasons. These projections could pave the way for the development of pressure- or strain-controlled, Tellurene-based quantum devices. Lastly, we explored the potential for stacking multiple quantum-wells made from different materials with both trivial and non-trivial properties, anticipating this could facilitate the creation of universal, threshold-based quantum phase transition materials. These advancements could, in turn, contribute to the development of multifunctional, quantum material membranes.

This paper examines the spin-valve characteristics of a nanowire made of ferromagnetic material, specifically GaMnAs, with two distinct types of terminals having different exchange coupling strengths. Our findings show that mild exchange fields trigger significant control over the spin-valve response, while stronger fields lead to partial loss of control due to tunneling decay. Experimental results demonstrate that the spin-valve current can be controlled through moderate exchange fields, achieving a substantial on-off ratio even at relatively low fields. This effect originates from the differing magnetization orientations of the two terminals, where their close exchange coupling causes one to overcome the other at moderate fields, resulting in a cumulative effect that reverses the spin-valve current. This phenomenon yields an on-off ratio of over 2 and a near-zero voltage when the more strongly coupled terminal has a higher magnetization, all occurring at moderately low exchange fields. This magnetic control of the spin-valve current could enable the development of multi-terminal spin-valve devices capable of accurate quantification of magnetization strength. Furthermore, combining this concept with spin-polarized light could provide a more precise method of exchange field measurement. Additionally, our research suggests that the spin-valve current can be employed to counteract undesirable spin-valve currents caused by the spin polarization of light, such as in solar cells or optical sensors, by applying a specific exchange field. Consequently, this concept has the potential to enhance the performance of such devices. In traditional neural network training, errors in individual neurons are averaged to create a global loss function, which is then utilized to adjust the weights. To improve training efficiency, a method involving the incorporation of adversarial factors is proposed. The proposed framework's performance is evaluated through several applications, and the results show significant improvements over conventional methods. Furthermore, to facilitate training, a method involving the reduction of dimensions is also explored, and the results show that it enables the solution of complex inverse problems involving grid systems with millions of degrees of freedom. To facilitate collaboration and knowledge sharing, the proposed framework's code is made openly available. Through numerical experiments, it is shown that the proposed framework can be applied to various contexts, including the solution of partial differential equations and statistical inversion problems. To further advance the field, several potential research directions are identified, and they are expected to enhance the performance of numerical models even further. This paper introduces a novel approach called protective training, aiming to prevent silent data corruptions in neural networks from the start. We observe that simply employing non-uniform filtering within the training data significantly enhances the robustness of a model, especially when applying more stringent filtering. This insight leads us to incorporate varied degree of restricted training, such as using different sizes of uniform random ranges or non-uniform regions, to further amplify the model's robustness. By incorporating multiple degrees of restricted training into a protective training scheme, we demonstrate significant improvements in the fundamental robustness benchmark - the ability of a model to operate accurately even in the presence of silent data corruptions. We also showcase how this method achieves higher performance than previous techniques combining noise injection and virtual multiple training. This method also achieves better performance than alternative approaches such as Endurance Training and highly customized models that are tailored to specific workload conditions. Lastly, we demonstrate the effectiveness of protective training on large-language-models and computer vision models. This paper explores the application of netting algorithms to connected graphs, revealing that a simple sorted approach can solve the problem efficiently. This finding is grounded in a basic example and subsequently expanded to handle negative weights. By building upon previous work and introducing new concepts, we aim to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding netting algorithms. This framework can serve as a foundation for further innovations in this area. Additionally, we clarify that many previous netting algorithms can be viewed as instances of this framework. This study introduces a novel approach for name-tagging in languages with limited data, utilizing a type-driven model that incorporates character-level markings. Unlike conventional sequence-tagging methods, this model labels characters rather than predicting sequence classifications, which has been shown to be an effective strategy in low-data settings. However, this approach typically requires substantial training data and high-quality annotations. To overcome these challenges, we propose a method that utilizes partial character-level labeling and a character-level regularization technique known as multi-head average, which has been successful in low-data settings. Additionally, we incorporate a type-driven model that leverages partial name patterns as additional input, allowing for improved performance in low-data settings. To evaluate this approach, we created a dataset for identifying names in Portuguese, which includes partial character-level and sequence-level annotations, and conducted experiments using this dataset and three other name-datasets in English, Chinese, and Arabic. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms previous methods in the Portuguese dataset and comparable performance to sequence-tagging models in the three other datasets. Our research examined various particle ratios in different collision systems and energies. By analyzing data from the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS experiments, we found that there are distinct trends in particle production patterns as the scale of the collision system shifts from small to large. Specifically, we observed that charged-particle multiplicity and transverse momentum measurements exhibit little differentiation across various collision systems, whereas particle ratios involving strange and heavy flavor particles demonstrate significant dependence on the collision system. Furthermore, our data reveals a gradual trend in particle production patterns as the energy of the collision increases from lower to higher levels, with some differences persisting in certain particle species even at the highest energy levels. Lastly, we discovered that collisions involving large systems of particles probe the properties of QCD matter at high temperatures and low densities, and that experiments need to accumulate significantly more data to observe subtle trends in strange and heavy flavor particle production. These findings provide a foundation for theoretical models that can be used to study the properties of QCD matter. Machine learning models, including dialogue state tracking models, can be susceptible to being influenced by noisy data. We investigate the impact of introducing labeled noise into a training dataset, specifically within the context of dialogue state tracking. Our research focuses on developing a robust model capable of reducing the effect of labeled noise. We create a dataset with intentionally incorrect labels and utilize the clean data from the SuperGLUE dataset to train and test our model. Our results show that by incorporating a small amount of clean data into the training process, the model can achieve better performance and be less affected by the labeled noise. We discovered that using a robust training method and averaging the results from multiple models can further enhance the model's resistance to labeled noise. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that a dialogue state tracking model can be trained to effectively cope with labeled errors by leveraging nearly clean training data. The code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/strmlab/Dialog-State-Tracking-Robustness.git

Given a set of real polynomials expressed as the sum of squares of other polynomials, the minimum number of these square polynomials can be quite high, especially when dealing with matrices and their associated algebraic invariants. A recent study introduced the concept of a Gram spectrahedron to tackle this challenge for a specific set of polynomials and matrices. Building upon this work, we propose an updated framework for the Gram spectrahedron that enables us to obtain a more efficient sum of squares decomposition for a broader range of polynomials and matrices. This improvement comes with the cost of potentially using more square polynomials, although it still offers significant benefits in certain scenarios. The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows. Firstly, we obtain an alternative expression for the $k$-rank of the Gram spectrahedron, denoted as $\Sigma_k$, in terms of the $k$-rank of another related spectrahedron. Secondly, we establish a connection between the number of polynomials in a sum of squares decomposition and the rank of matrices within the Gram spectrahedron. Lastly, we explore several specific cases where we are able to determine the minimum number of polynomials required for a sum of squares decomposition. Notably, we find that this minimum number can be expressed as a linear combination of certain algebraic invariants of the matrix in question. Lastly, we provide a lower bound for the number of polynomials in a sum of squares decomposition, which scales linearly with the rank of the matrix. This finding has implications for the study of convex projects of the Gram spectrahedron. Lastly, we discuss several open questions related to the generalised problem. The FASERν experiment at CERN aims to investigate rare neutrino interactions by analyzing the neutrino background originating from the decay of beauty and charm mesons produced in the LHCb beam interaction with the Earth's crust. Due to its unique location and timing, this experiment can also provide notable constraints on leptonic non-unitarity parameters beyond the established CKM unitarity constraints. In this study, we evaluate the sensitivity of the FASERν experiment to various non-unitarity parameters such as $|U_{\mu \tau}|^2$ and $\Delta F=2$ processes for muons and taons, also considering the LHCb's contribution. Furthermore, we compare the expected constraints from FASERν to the existing bounds on these parameters, indicating that FASERν can significantly improve the current understanding of these processes. In particular, we find that FASERν can tighten the unitarity error for the muon sector by a factor of at least five, and potentially improve the unitarity error for the tau sector by a factor of twenty. Additionally, we find that FASERν can reduce the current 90% confidence interval for $|U_{\mu \tau}|^2$ from the range $[0.12, 0.56]$ to $0.35\pm0.06$, and for $\Delta F=2$ processes, FASERν can lower the 90% confidence interval for $\Delta \bar{K}^0$ to $[-0.60, 0.00)$ and for $\Delta \bar{C}^0$ to $[-0.26, 0.00)$. We introduce a novel perspective on the knowledge amalgamation problem, which involves a student model learning from multiple instructor models. A saliency-based method is proposed to identify the most effective combinations of instructor models, by highlighting the knowledge areas where the student will gain the most from. To achieve this, we incorporate an attention mechanism into the amalgamation process. Instead of selecting all instructor models, the student now focuses on a subset of them, where each one contributes unique insight to the desired knowledge area. As a result, the student can be trained efficiently on this reduced subset, leading to faster and more effective learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method through both theoretical and practical evaluations, showing that it not only outperforms the current state-of-the-art but also achieves remarkable performance with a significantly smaller dataset. The code for the proposed method is openly available on GitHub. Although the brain's spatial coding system relies heavily on grid cells with precisely spaced activation patterns, research has shown that these cells can compensate with similar patterns using external sensory inputs to determine a animal's position. However, a different strategy is employed by the insect brain's navigation system, which uses distinct neural networks for processing visual and olfactory sensors to determine where an animal is based on various environmental features. This study investigates a combined approach in the insect brain, where grid cells are triggered by two separate inputs: one from a wide-angle visual sensor that monitors an animal's surroundings and another from an animal's sense of direction while navigating through a narrow path. By combining these inputs, a mathematical model shows that grid cells with precisely spaced activation patterns can be generated without relying on periodic stimuli in a simulated environment that is periodically varied. Furthermore, this model suggests that the integrity of activation patterns is robust against minor disturbances and can be reconfigured to respond to changes in the type of sensory input used, such as switching from vision to olfaction. Additionally, when the model is subjected to a moving grid environment, periodic slow variations in the system's parameters cause a phenomenon known as "fractional localization", where activation patterns are retained but with additional spatial periodicities related to the rate of change. As a result, the model predicts that in a genuine biological system, the integrity of grid cells could be tested under conditions of fractional localization. Also, it is suggested that the complexity of grid cells with multiple spatial periodicities could be a consequence of the interaction between the brain's spatial coding system and the complex sensory inputs it receives. External validity of this idea is supported by research showing that the response of insect grid cells to visual stimuli resembles fractional localization in a simulated moving grid environment. Ultimately, this study indicates that the dependence of grid cells on external cues is an inevitable consequence of the interaction between the brain's spatial coding system and the complex sensory inputs it receives, with implications for a deeper understanding of the biological validity of navigation systems. The area where kinematic dynamos have an impact on magnetic cycles in stars that rotate slowly is not yet fully understood. Kinematic dynamos drive magnetic field buildup without being reinforced by electrodynamic feedback. The effect of a kinematic dynamo on magnetic cycles is illustrated using a simplified model, which includes an oscillatory activity source and a nonlinear feedback loop found in turbulent flows, and is applied to stars that rotate slowly. The result shows that kinematic dynamos can cause magnetic cycles, but only if the rotation rate is high enough to allow for the extraction of free energy from the shear stress of differential rotation. If the rotation is too slow, kinetic dynamos will dominate, and the kinematic dynamo's cycle will be suppressed. The scenario in which kinematic dynamos contribute to magnetic cycles applies to stars that rotate between one tenth and one quarter of the solar rotation rate. The influence of convective flux reversals on these kinematic dynamos is examined, and it is found that when these reversals are nonlinear, they can stimulate magnetic cycles. However, when the reversals are linear, they will not stimulate magnetic cycles. We investigate the time-dependent production of entropy during a quantum change known as a "quench," which involves suddenly changing the parameters of a model called the XXI chain. This change causes a sudden increase in entropy, and we study how it affects the difference between initial and final entropies, as well as a related measurement called the "temperature." Our analysis is based on calculations using a method called the thermodynamic Bethe ansatz, and our results show complex patterns in both entropy and temperature as they change over time. Conversely, a simpler model allows us to analyze the quench by comparing it to another change known as a "slow change," and we find that both entropy and temperature exhibit similar patterns in both cases. This leads to an important discovery that the time-dependent production of entropy during a quench is directly proportional to the difference between initial and final temperatures, and can be expressed by a universal formula that is independent of the specific characteristics of the system being studied. This finding represents a key advancement in understanding the time-dependent production of entropy, and has significant implications for our knowledge of quantum systems, particularly those that exhibit long periods of thermal behavior known as "Luther-Emery phases." Lastly, our results have implications for our understanding of quantum systems in a state of "quantum chaos," and provide a mathematical connection between these systems and their counterparts in a state of "thermal chaos."

We explore the concept of time-twirling in non-unitary dynamics, which involves identifying environments that make the associated dynamical map indistinguishable from unitary evolution over a certain period. This investigation reveals that the time-twirling of an initial state involves averaging its evolution under various environments, with the average being taken over all non-unitary channels that preserve symmetry. We demonstrate that such time-twirling is equivalent to selecting a subset of unitary channels and then averaging only those subsets, which facilitates our primary contribution. This contribution is particularly significant because it provides a lower bound for the time-twirling of an initial state's distinguishability from unitary evolution, which occurs at a specific point in time and is applicable even when the initial state has a particular symmetry. This ground state can be obtained through the time-twirling of a superposition of ground states, with the superposition being highly entangled and coherent. Furthermore, this research reveals that time-twirling is an extensive property, which implies that it increases with the addition of new, independent systems, regardless of those systems being entangled with the original environment or not. Consequently, this extensive property of time-twirling is in line with the principles of typicality, which is further highlighted by comparing our findings with the typical subspace in the context of unitary evolution. Ultimately, our findings provide a new perspective on the study of time-twirling in non-unitary dynamics and facilitate the exploration of extensive properties in line with the principles of typicality. Moreover, this research paves the way for investigating questions about the coherence of time-twilled states and the vastness of time-twilled subspaces in complex systems. Lastly, our study opens up possibilities for experimenting with time-twilling in real-world experiments involving non-unitary dynamics. These experiments could involve controlling the evolution of systems in scenarios such as the loss of quantum states in optical free-space communication, the decay of superposed states in quantum computations, or the evolution of entangled states in quantum simulations, among others. Additionally, our research offers the potential to distinguish unitary from non-unitary evolution in complex systems through interference experiments involving multiple environments. Ultimately, our study on time-twilling in non-unitary dynamics may lead to breakthroughs in understanding the principles of unitary evolution in complex systems. We examine the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex within a unit cube $Q_n$ with interpolation nodes. Specifically, we investigate the condition $\binom{n+1}{2} \leq |X|$ for the unit cube $Q_n$. Our analysis reveals that when the number of interpolation nodes exceeds $\binom{n+1}{2}$, a nondegenerate regular simplex in $Q_n$ is certain. Conversely, we demonstrate that for $n \geq 3$, there exists a set of interpolation nodes in $Q_n$ satisfying the condition $\binom{n+1}{2} \leq |X|$, where no nondegenerate regular simplex in $Q_n$ exists. Additionally, we explore similar concepts within the context of a finite set of functions defined on $Q_n$. Finally, we discuss potential applications of our findings to the analysis of theorems involving polynomial interpolation methods. The type and concentration of carriers in etched silicon can be manipulated through the use of various surface modification techniques. This study compares the carrier concentration in etched silicon obtained via two methods: etching the silicon itself and etching the buffer oxide layer on top of the silicon. The results show that carrier concentration in etched silicon is significantly higher when the silicon itself is etched, with values ranging from 10^20 to 10^21 cm^-3. In contrast, carrier concentration in etched buffer oxide layer is much lower, ranging from 2.5*10^17 to 8*10^18 cm^-3. The higher carrier concentration in etched silicon is attributed to the formation of nanosized hydrogenated silicon clusters with a small size, which can lead to quantum confinement and a significant increase in carrier concentration. The formation of these clusters is believed to occur because etching silicon itself allows for the local release of strain between adjacent atoms, which can lead to the formation of Si-Si bonds and the accumulation of additional carriers. The proposed model is further supported by the observation that the formation of these clusters is inhibited when the buffer oxide layer is etched, likely due to the presence of hydrogen atoms in that case, which can occupy dangling silicon bonds and prevent the formation of Si-Si bonds. The findings of this study provide a new perspective on the formation of carriers in etched silicon and may have significant implications for the development of silicon-based technology, including solar cells, thermoelectric devices, and sensors. Furthermore, the proposed model offers a potential solution to the doping limit in silicon, which has been a longstanding challenge in the field. The results of this study are validated through the use of theoretical simulations, which show good agreement with the experimental data. The most highly strained areas with low hydrogen content were found to have the highest carrier concentrations, which is consistent with the proposed model. This water is thought to have been released into the atmosphere during various planetary processes, including mantle convection and the cycling of water between the interior and exterior of the planet. In turn, the atmosphere may, in theory, impact the mantle through a process known as atmospheric mantle feedback, potentially affecting the Earth's climate and geology over time. Our theoretical analysis employs multi-level scattering models to investigate the methyl ion production efficiencies in propanediol (PDO) isomers, specifically 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO. Our method considers the scattering of water molecules with PDO molecules at different temperature levels, as described by the Boltzmann distribution, and evaluates the resulting complex stability using energy barriers. We found that 1,2-PDO yields a more stable methyl ion complex due to the formation of two N-H$\ldots$O hydrogen bonds with a water molecule, which facilitates water molecule desorption, thereby increasing the efficiency of methyl ion production. In contrast, 1,3-PDO forms a more stable complex with two water molecules, which reduces the efficiency of methyl ion production. This difference in complex structure explains the higher methyl ion production efficiency observed experimentally for 1,2-PDO compared to 1,3-PDO. We also determined that water molecule desorption is the rate-determining step in the production of methyl ions from PDO. Our approach can be applied to analyze the production of other organic ions from various alcohols and sugars. Nevertheless, the water molecule desorption often becomes the rate-determining step, which is influenced by the specific structure of the sugar molecule or alcohol. In some cases, the efficiency of complex formation with sugar molecules or alcohols can further impact the water molecule desorption process. Ultimately, our study provides a theoretical basis for understanding the unique reactivity of PDO and other organic compounds in water. It also offers a new perspective on the ongoing debate regarding the origin of methyl ion production in PDO, with some researchers attributing it to molecular scattering and others to chemical reactions involving hydroxymethyl groups. Our approach combines both views, suggesting that the efficiency of methyl ion production from PDO depends on the water molecule desorption process, which is influenced by the complex structure formed between PDO molecules and water molecules and, therefore, can be affected by the method of PDO formation. In consequence, the prevalence of 1,2-PDO over 1,3-PDO becomes the primary factor explaining the higher methyl ion production efficiency observed experimentally for 1,2-PDO. Our study explores a novel method of converting any tensor network into a PQC, focusing on the specific case of matrix product states (MPS). We demonstrate that our proposed framework successfully retains the original accuracy and offers a notably more compact description of the system - one that outperforms prior methods by achieving the lowest possible number of circuit parameters. We further illustrate the advantages of our conversion approach through the tangible improvement it induces in the training processes of quantum circuit learning (QCL). Ultimately, our research reveals that, regardless of the intricacy of the system, our conversion technique consistently produces shallow PQCs, which can be deeply folded into circuit architectures possessing hierarchical structure and exhibiting both entanglement swapping and multi-body interactions. We envision the benefits of our method extending beyond the realm of tensor network algorithms to any situation where understanding well-entangled states is crucial. We hope this research paves the way for the development of more efficient QCL protocols that can accurately describe complex, multi-body physics by only tuning a small number of parameters. To accelerate the computation of gravitational interactions in numerically resolved simulations of astrophysical systems, our research introduces a modified version of the Fast Multipole Method (FMM). Typically, FMM is utilized in simulations of gravitational interactions within a fixed, three-dimensional domain. In contrast, simulations of astrophysical systems often require a broader perspective, encompassing an extensive range of scales from a few parsecs to thousands of parsecs. As a result, incorporating FMM into these simulations poses significant computational challenges. To tackle these difficulties, we developed a recursive, eight-dimensional algorithm for calculating gravitational interactions and demonstrated that this approach offers an order of magnitude improvement in computational efficiency for certain scale hierarchies. Furthermore, we successfully applied this method to tackle the complexities of hierarchical astrophysical systems and incorporated it into the Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) framework used for these simulations. By leveraging AMR and the modified FMM, we were able to accelerate the computation of gravitational interactions by approximately three orders of magnitude, thereby enabling more detailed resolutions of astrophysical systems and longer simulation timelines. As a result, we have taken a significant step towards developing a computationally efficient tool that can thoroughly examine the dynamics of astrophysical systems over extensive scales. However, given the numerous innovations required to tackle these challenges, we also acknowledge the necessity for continuous improvement and openness to suggestions and contributions from the scientific community. As such, we are presenting the first public version of our project, along with the source code and data that accompanies it, in the hope of fostering collaboration and contributing to the advancement of this project. This paper introduces a novel contrastive learning algorithm for cross-anatomy domain adaptation, which enables the segmentation of complex anatomical structures. By incorporating semi-supervised learning, our method enhances the adaptation capability by introducing similar and distinct sample pairs in both source and target domains. We utilize a dual classification network to classify samples as similar or distinct, which also allows for the generation of target domain labels. This contrastive loss and label loss are combined to train the network through alternating least squares. Our CS-CADA approach demonstrates superior performance compared to existing domain adaptation methods in the challenging BrainTumors segmentation task. The code and models are available online for download.

We discover that an anomalous BRS symmetry allows for the resolution of 3+1 dimensional supergravity, ultimately leading to a revision of the supergravity principle. By incorporating a specific BRS anomalous term in the action, we transform the BRS symmetry into a precise, long-lasting symmetry. This, in turn, enables the derivation of a novel Yang-Mills field equation, in close resemblance to the Bekenstein-Hawking formula for gravity. A novel dimension formula emerges from this equation, featuring an adjustment term related to the BRS anomalous dimension. We also establish the relationship between the BRS anomalous dimension and the conformal one, leading to the conclusion that the conformal dimension is irrelevant. Instead, it is the BRS anomalous dimension that assumes paramount importance in the context of supergravity. This development paves the way for a revised supergravity principle, where the BRS anomalous dimension plays a crucial role in defining the algebra of supergravity. This new perspective on supergravity may have a broader implications for theories that involve the Yang-Mills field. Moreover, we propose the introduction of a fictitious BRS anomalous dimension to solve the Gribov problem within the Yang-Mills theory. Finally, we explore the phenomenon of supergravity becoming a Yang-Mills type of theory after the introduction of an appropriate BRS anomalous term, specifically in the context of the holographic duality. Here, we discuss the potential for this idea to contribute to a deeper comprehension of the Higgs mechanism. Ultimately, our study indicates that introducing an anomalous BRS term yields a precise, long-lasting BRS symmetry within 3+1 dimensional supergravity, allowing us to derive novel Yang-Mills and gravity field equations. analyze the ability of the swimmer to transition between any two given
positions, and determine the frequency of switching that optimizes this
transition under a constraint of constant force. The effectiveness of this
optimization is confirmed through simulations, and we observe that in some
instances, the optimal strategy involves simply moving in the direction
indicated by the force vector. A comparison between swimmers with different
joint complexities reveals that their relative performance varies depending on
the level of force applied. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a swimmer with
passive joints can outperform one with active joints in specific scenarios. 
This research provides the foundation for investigating how external forces
and environmental conditions influence the performance of swimmers with passive
joints. The associated benefits and drawbacks are also discussed. 
Finally, possible applications for this study are mentioned in the context
of robotic systems that navigate through fluid with limited power.

The spread of fake news through social media is a pressing concern, and machine learning models that can identify and help mitigate this issue have gained significance. Most existing research has been focused on developing models that utilize isolation-based information, ignoring the significance of contextual data. This study challenges this prevailing mindset with a counter-intuitive hypothesis that contextual information plays a crucial role in determining whether a particular piece of information constitutes fake news or not. To test this hypothesis, we created a new dataset called CiNews, which incorporates contextual information drawn from the title and opposite article content for decision-making. The study further compares the performance differences between models trained on isolation-based and context-aided information, yielding surprising results that context-aided information does not necessarily lead to improved outcomes. Instead, our findings indicate that models can be robust in situations where contextual information is limited, which is demonstrated through additional experiments showcasing the impact of diverse context on model performance. The study's counter-intuitive findings challenge the existing narrative on the importance of contextual information in determining fake news and provide a new perspective on the topic. Moreover, our findings suggest that models can excel in scenarios with limited context-aided information, yielding performance comparable to that achieved with isolation-based information. Lastly, we explore the phenomenon of robust modeling by experimenting with models that can handle disparate context, which lays the groundwork for further exploration in this area. Although it enables consistent labeling without additional annotations, the current evaluation methods are limited to basic metrics such as F-score. In this study, we introduce a framework that incorporates paraphrasing to validate the consistency of annotated labels and propose a novel evaluation method. This proposal involves refining the evaluation process by comparing the semantics of original and paraphased text. Additionally, we incorporate a word mismatch metric to evaluate the consistency of annotations. When put to the test on previously collected datasets, our proposed framework demonstrates superior performance in evaluating the consistency of annotations compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we achieve notable improvements in accuracy on the STVC dataset after implementing our proposed framework. Notably, our results indicate significant reductions in both precision and recall errors, resulting in overall F-score errors that are nearly indistinguishable from those produced by fully supervised training methods. Our framework also demonstrates exceptional scalability, capable of processing over 1,800 sentences per hour on a single GPU. X-ray spectra from the Europlexus archive have been analyzed for a group of 13 cataclysmic variables, including nine polars and four asynchronous polars without detectable X-ray pulsations. The study reveals that asynchronous polars display similar X-ray spectra to standard polars, indicating that magnetic field strength has an insignificant impact on the presence of low-energy X-ray radiation. The spectrum of low-energy X-rays in cataclysmic variables is largely independent of the type of white dwarf and is not significantly influenced by the presence of an accretion disk or global pulsations. The study also shows that X-ray spectra of cataclysmic variables are consistent with thermal emission from a population of colliding winds within the disk, and that magnetic field strength is unlikely to significantly influence this behavior. The study further suggests that the majority of X-ray pulsations in cataclysmic variables are a result of global pulsations being observed, and that magnetic field strength has an insignificant impact on the behavior of global pulsations. The study includes the analysis of the aluminum K-shell line at 1.83 keV, which was previously overlooked in the interpretation of X-ray spectra of cataclysmic variables. In fluid-structure interaction (FSI) applications, a common strategy is to split the simulation into two components, solving the fluid and solid problems separately within each time step. We examine the requirements and challenges of developing a flexible numerical framework for these problems, focusing on developing a suite of solvers that can be divided into three layers: problem solvers for individual components and a coupling layer that integrates them. Through this structure, various numerical approaches for the fluid and solid problems can be easily exchanged without rewriting the coupling layer, which remains problem-agnostic. To demonstrate this approach, we develop a simple partitioned FSI application using Python, leveraging the FEniCS platform for the spatial resolution of the fluid and solid equations. To enhance stability, a first-order implicit method is applied to the coupling layer, and we demonstrate the simulation of a benchmark RANS-SES case to showcase the framework's capabilities. To further showcase the framework's flexibility, we successfully integrate an existing solver for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, implementing the CUBIT meshing tool to generate models and a basic Python script for the coupling layer. Furthermore, we successfully integrate this combined model with the RANS-SES application. Local metric maps within mapping frameworks like SLAM have been extensively explored, however the concept of global metric maps has not received substantial attention. A recent approach known as HiTMap proposes a global metric map representation, albeit with minimal focus on method development. This paper provides an alternative, nuanced take on HiTMap and presents a corresponding state estimation technique. Our representation, termed HiTMap in its broad sense, comprises a variety of tools for navigating through paired sensor data and projected scene images. This state estimation method is then applied to a hypothetical scenario featuring a mobile device navigating across multiple tables. Our results show that our approach allows for efficient navigation and accurate state estimation, both with and without visual information. A practical demonstration involves the use of a 3D printer to create physical global metric maps in the form of curved surfaces. These printed maps can be navigated by a robotic device equipped with HiTMap. Our code has been made publicly accessible on the GitHub platform.

This problem has been addressed by developing methods that estimate the weights as a Markov process, but these methods are computationally intensive and only applicable to continuous data attributes. Our research proposes a new method that leverages the characteristics of Dirichlet distributions to derive a closed-form expression for the posterior weights, effectively recasting them as a first-order Markov process. A theoretical model reveals that thin, low-density secondary layers can significantly enhance ion acceleration in negatively chirped regions, even when these layers are much thinner than the laser's ensembles. This could potentially lead to the development of highly efficient, compact ion sources. We investigate this precision when measuring the mass of an object using qubits and qutrits and find that qutrits can measure mass with greater tolerance to noise than qubits, especially when measuring the mass directly. However, when measuring mass indirectly, qutrits' greater noise tolerance to measurement precision is conditional upon specific error channels. We develop a theoretical framework to quantify the trade-off between measuring the mass directly or indirectly and analyze various error channels that affect this precision. Our study provides a foundation for exploring the measure precision in higher-dimensional systems. Furthermore, our findings suggest that qutrits could offer a threshold for achieving more precise mass measurement with less necessary measurement and could potentially facilitate the development of more complex operations in quantum physics with higher-dimensional systems. Our research also highlights the potential for contributing to the development of quantum metrology, specifically in the application of quark physics, and lays a theoretical groundwork for investigating precision measurement in higher-dimensional systems. The framework we introduced could as well be applicable to other fields like communication and cryptography. In stars, the magnetic field plays a significant role in their rotation, activity, and mass loss, influencing their evolution and impact on surrounding planets. Research has shown that stable, long-lasting magnetic fields in non-bipolar configurations require the cancellation of two modes: toroidal and poloidal. These modes can be linked through a helical magnetic axis, which is a characteristic feature of stellar magnetic fields. Based on an asymptotic expansion of magnetic free energy, a simple model reveals that the interaction between toroidal and poloidal modes, when helical symmetry is considered, can stabilize the star against non-axisymmetric instabilities in certain cases. However, when this balance is broken, either by a change in the star or its magnetic field, the instability can occur. The study also finds that the rotation rate of the star has a modest effect on the instability threshold, while the helical symmetry of the magnetic field has a significant influence. This research provides a theoretical basis for understanding the stability of magnetic fields in antennas, T Tauri stars, and solar-type stars, and offers implications for the behavior of massive stars and stellar mergers. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of studying the magnetic fields in these objects. For example, if the toroidal mode dominates in the solar-type stars, it is possible that the solar giant convective rolls could be stimulated by this mode. Additionally, in massive stars, where the toroidal mode may dominate, it could influence their conventional mixing patterns, either enhancing or suppressing the mixing, depending on the location, and potentially leading to the appearance of chemical abundance patterns that are similar to those found in the products of massive star mergers. The findings of this research are also applicable to the stellar mergers, such as GW470386, which exhibited a significant toroidal magnetic field, and GW403226, which had a dominant poloidal magnetic field. The study suggests that the mergers with dominant poloidal magnetic fields may exhibit stable, long-lasting magnetic fields, while those with dominant toroidal magnetic fields may have unstable magnetic fields, leading to the cancellation of the magnetic field shortly after the merger. The research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the stability of magnetic fields in antennas, T Tauri stars, solar-type stars, massive stars, and the stars formed as a result of stellar mergers, offering a range of predictions that can be tested by the upcoming generation of stellar magnetic field surveys. Building on the work of Conway and Saper, we define a concept of topological groupoid extension that aligns with gerbes over topological stacks. This framework provides a natural language for describing the local structure of the stack of gerbes on a topological stack. By incorporating a vanishing cohomology class, our theory expands upon Conway and Saper's findings, allowing us to identify a one-to-one correspondence between isomorphism classes of gerbes on a stack and the isomorphism classes of twisted maps from its classifying space to the classifying space of the group that gerbes represent. This correspondence enables us to compute the classifying space of the gerbe of gerbes on a stack. As a result, we derive the expression for the Chern-Connes-Immersioni invariant of a stack through its classifying space and the Chern class of the gerbe of gerbes. This approach offers a geometric interpretation of this invariant, and it further enables us to establish the divisibility properties predicted by Galski in the special case of complex analytic stacks. Finally, we establish the connection between the ring structure of the Chern-Connes-Immersioni invariant and the ring structure of the holomorphic cohomology ring via the Gaiffman-Hatcher reconstruction theorem. The formation of massive stars is a priority area in the study of molecular cores with significant mass potential. This study's original database consists of 1157 cores selected from the ATLAS/GLASP molecular core catalog, using observed star formation rates and far-infrared color temperatures as indicators. The database includes core properties such as mass, size, density, and the presence of outflows, protostars, and far-infrared point sources. By tracking core masses over a three-year period, this study reveals a mass growth distribution that can be modelled by a power-law with a 4:3 exponent. Approximately 70% of cores with masses above 1000 times that of the sun's mass and a small radius remain massive over the observed period, while about 30% of these massive cores have a larger size and lower density, suggesting they could be high-mass starless cores. Only 13% of cores with densities above 10 to the power of -6 grams per cubic centimeter and masses above 100 times that of the sun's mass have a large size and remain massive over the observed period, and only 10% of these cores have a density above 10 to the power of -5 grams per cubic centimeter. Interestingly, core densities generally decline over time, indicating that density is not the primary factor in the continuation of high-mass starless core status. Instead, it appears that large low-density high-mass cores have a higher chance of remaining high-mass starless cores, likely because they are closer to their final mass and have fewer channels for mass loss, such as outflows and protostar formation. This research provides a larger statistical sample size than previous studies and offers a more comprehensive understanding of the mass growth of high-mass starless cores, a crucial phase in the formation of massive stars. It also highlights the importance of observing high-mass starless cores over extended periods and conducting follow-up studies to determine the outcome of these cores. It is hoped that this research will contribute to the development of models that can accurately predict the formation of massive stars from high-mass starless cores.
