Finite Godel algebras of size $n$ are isomorphic to the forest algebras of size $n$, and this characterization leads to a new polynomial identity of degree $2n$ in three variables, which is known to be the most concise form of the finite Godel algebras' identity by Reynolds. This paper goes on to explore a more general context, considering algebras that satisfy the finite Godel identity along with the identity of forest algebras, and such algebras can be viewed as an extension of finite Godel algebras. These algebras of size $n$ are then shown to be dual to the forest algebras of size $n$, and as a result, they can be viewed as the bivariant functions from the forest algebras of size $n$ to the set containing two elements. Furthermore, this context allows for the introduction of a more general notion of Kleene algebras. However, the paper then shows that the combination of the finite Godel identity and the identity of forest algebras is equivalent to the combination of the finite Boolean algebra and the finite Kleene algebras' identities, and this combination is not finitely based. This means that any algebra that satisfies this combination will also satisfy the combination of the finite Boolean algebra and the finite Kleene algebras' identities. This result is then applied to the context of partial algebras, and it is shown that the combination of the finite Godel identity and the identity of forest algebras is not finitely based in this context either. This research is then connected to its broader context, discussing recent developments in the field. Finally, some open questions are proposed. This paper is intended to honor the scientific legacies of H. A. Kitchens and his son J. Kitchens, who have both made significant contributions to the field. This contribution is in the form of an extensive review of recent research, accompanied by fresh open questions in the field of algebra. This review is particularly focused on the context of finite Godel algebras and their associated identities, and it is accompanied by two newly proposed questions. This paper is the second part of a larger series, and it is followed by Part III, which is also available separately. This research is connected to the 2019 ARITA conference held in Otago, New Zealand. This paper ultimately aims to provide an overview of the current state of the field, accompanied by fresh perspectives and questions in the area

The long-term stability of liquid foams typically depends on two key factors: the surface tension and the viscosity of the liquid films, and a roughness factor that accounts for the complexity of film interactions as they dry and change shape. Although the importance of the roughness factor has only recently been fully acknowledged, it has a profound impact on the behavior of liquid foams, influencing how quickly and far they can be pushed before breaking apart. In this study, a new method of measuring the roughness factor has been developed, involving the use of a instrument that applies increasing stress to a plate with a layer of liquid foam attached, until the foam ultimately ruptures. The results of this method were validated by comparing them to a established technique, and showed a good level of accuracy when measured in the same way. The new method was then tested on a variety of different liquids, including beer and milk, showing it to be a quick and reliable way of determining the roughness factor. This will be an important tool for scientists who study the behavior of liquid foams, as it will allow them to better understand the complex forces at play when a foam is subjected to stress and pressure. In our research, we aim to enhance convolutional neural network (CNN) performance on image classification tasks using ensemble learning. By combining multiple CNN models with diverse architecture components, we achieve a notable improvement in accuracy. The complex model is divided into sub-modules, and each module's performance is optimized on a dataset subset. We evaluated our method on the fundamental image classification dataset, CIFAR-10, and attained a maximum accuracy of 90.45%, surpassing the baseline CNN model accuracy of 82.53%. We also successfully applied this ensemble approach to the more complex dataset, FLIC, which consists of medical images, and observed a significant increase in accuracy of 8.43% over the baseline. We investigate the idea of quantizing thermodynamic fields by examining the behavior of a single particle within a harmonic oscillator at finite temperatures. Our analysis focuses on working rather than heat transfer, which allows us to develop an understanding of thermodynamic processes through the evolution of microstates. We find that time-dependent microstates perform complete cycles in phase space, and by calculating the average work done during these cycles, we determine the mean value of dissipated work. Our results show that the mean dissipated work is directly proportional to the Boltzmann constant and is linked to the ratio of the classical action to the Planck constant, and can be expressed as a stochastic action. This study provides a framework for understanding the quantization of thermodynamic fields and reveals a connection between the quantization of work and the behavior of electrons in periodic potentials. Our research also indicates that the mean dissipated work is a fundamental property of closed classical systems undergoing cyclic changes and can be derived independently of Maxwell's demon. Finally, we explore the relationship between our results and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. By examining the specific case of an electric current in a resistor, we find that the mean dissipated work done by the microstate on the system is equal to the product of the resistance, the square of the amplitude of the oscillation, and the frequency of the vibration. This result is in line with the prediction made by the theory of optical faraday rotation in ferromagnetic materials. Moreover, our predictions can be tested using existing experimental data, and we anticipate that our research will contribute to a fresh perspective on the field of thermodynamics inspired by quantum mechanics. Additionally, we hope that our work will lead to an exploration of new phenomena related to the quantization of thermodynamic fields. A proposed attention mechanism in neural machine translation, known as look-ahead attention, considers both the current sentence's elements and those of the subsequent sentence. This suggested method involves modifying the attention mechanism to simultaneously process multiple sentences. However, implementing this would require significant computational costs. To mitigate this, we suggest a more efficient approach using a restricted look-ahead attention model, which is tested on two datasets and demonstrates improved performance. The proposed model is particularly effective in translating longer sentences. The suggested method also facilitates new perspectives on the attention mechanism, including the distribution of attention across sentences. This is accompanied by a publicly accessible repository containing the model's code. The proposed method's results, alongside an analysis of model performance, are presented in experiments conducted on the NIST Contextual Paragraph Translation Antonyms Task and the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task. This involves comparing the proposed method to both standard attention models and look-ahead attention models with full attention. The results indicate that the proposed method surpasses standard attention models, while incurring minimal additional computational costs. The model's performance is on par with the look-ahead attention model, which requires substantial computational resources. This efficiency comes from the proposed method's ability to process individual sentences independently, while maintaining parallelization capabilities. The method also fosters new insights into attention distribution, revealing a clear distinction between reading the current sentence and processing the subsequent sentence. This is accompanied by varying degrees of attention towards the current sentence's beginning, middle, and end. Overall, the proposed method provides a compelling solution for translating longer sentences and is readily available for use in neural machine translation applications. This study aims to further understand how peers affect curiosity through sharing and discovery in online communities. By examining interactions in Wikipedia's revision history, our analysis reveals that users' curiosity is often sparked by edits to articles they have not previously looked at. Furthermore, our results show that the frequency of users visiting pages that have been recently updated is higher when compared to older pages that have recently been modified. This effect is seen across various categories of Wikipedia articles. Additionally, our analysis indicates that users' curiosity is particularly piqued by updates to pages that have been recently visited by others, suggesting that social influences play a significant role in driving curiosity. This is particularly evident when considering the varying speeds at which users explore Wikipedia's site. Our results demonstrate that users' curiosity for updating pages is best predicted by factors such as the time since their last visit and whether the user has visited the page before, rather than relying on older measures that consider the age of the page itself. This study's findings provide a foundation for examining curiosity within online communities and can be applied to other collaborative environments, such as social networks. By understanding the drivers of curiosity in these settings, developers may be able to enhance experience exploration and discovery. We introduce GraphMatérnGP, an efficient framework for computing Gaussian process posteriors in non-conjugate, mini-batch settings utilizing graph convolutional networks. Currently, Gaussian process models are primarily limited to semi-conjugate extensions or pseudo steps due to their rigorous matrix nature. Our framework significantly broadens the application spectrum of graph Matérn Gaussian processes to any model that can be trained with stochastic gradient descent, enabling deep neural network training. Our innovative solution leverages z-normalized feature maps and incorporates batch normalization to both speed up computations and facilitate mini-batch learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by incorporating GraphMatérnGP into standard neural network modules, showcasing notable performance improvements on diverse dataset benchmarks. Our framework also extends the Matérn Gaussian process framework to various kernel combinations and multi-task learning scenarios. Our code is openly accessible and showcases the efficiency of our graph Matérn Gaussian process posterior computation, achieving a 5 times speed increase over traditional methods while reducing memory consumption by half. In monitoring the movement of objects and changes in the urban environment, a network of sensors mounted on ridesourcing vehicles can provide valuable and cost-effective coverage. However, the reliability of this sensing system is compromised because the sensors may infrequently observe certain areas. To improve both the coverage and reliability of this system, optimizations can be performed to reduce the time in which a section becomes visible to the sensors or to determine the most reliable sensor to update the view of an area. By framing these problems from the time an object is detected to its disappearance as variants of the $k$-cover and $k$-cover join problems, respectively, we can leverage developments in data stream research to find efficient solutions even when the sensor paths are partially known. Additionally, we contribute results to the $k$-cover and $k$-cover join problems over continuous data streams, and also examine the performance of these algorithms in simulation models of ridesourcing operations in major cities. Lastly, we discuss potential applications and future research paths for this sensing system, including the problem of minimizing costs in vehicle movements.

This paper delves into the mysteries of advanced algorithms used in automatic essay grading, which are increasingly employed by institutions to efficiently assess student performance. Despite their benefits, research has indicated that these algorithms can sometimes display inconsistent behavior, such as being overly sensitive to minor changes or resistant to significant alterations. To investigate this further, we analyzed a scoring model developed by one of the leading assessment providers, Vantage Learning, which utilizes deep learning. By conducting a thorough review of the model's code and testing its responses to various inputs, we uncovered instances of unstable and sensitive scoring. We also discovered that the model's evaluations could be manipulated by inserting irrelevant words, which can lead to inaccurate assessments. Our research suggests that educators and institutions must exercise extreme caution when relying on automatic grading systems, particularly if these systems are responsible for high-stakes decision-making. Furthermore, our findings highlight the importance of conducting rigorous testing and quality assurance for these systems to ensure their validity and reliability. Additionally, we propose that assessment providers should provide accessible code and engage with the research community to foster greater understanding of how these systems work. Ultimately, our research represents a crucial step towards developing more trustworthy automatic grading systems that are capable of making informed, human-like judgments. We have made our code and data set openly available, and we invite other researchers to join us in exploring the possibilities and limitations of these systems. We also hope that our work will spark a broader discussion about the use of artificial intelligence in assessment and its implications for higher education. We plan to build upon this research by investigating new methods of combining human and machine assessment, as well as exploring the conceptual foundations of assessment through the lens of critical theory. We hope that this will contribute to a more comprehensive and inclusive discussion about the future of assessment in higher education. This research investigates a random walk with independent and identically distributed zero-mean increments that may not be identically distributed, particularly focusing on its asymptotic behavior. The work builds upon earlier findings by Fyodorov and Bovivouk, which revealed that under certain conditions, the asymptotic distribution of the walk's position can be understood through the cumulative distribution function of a family of generalized gamma distributions. However, these conditions stipulated that the walks' increments must have a finite characteristic momentum, which can be interpreted as the character 'b' having a specific value that lies within a particular range. Now, unless the character 'b' is equal to 2, it is proven that the asymptotic distribution of the walk's position is not absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. Instead, it exhibits a distinct behavior characterized by a mixture of power laws, and this analysis holds without the constraint of finite characteristic momentum. Consequently, it is demonstrated that the character 'b' can be viewed as a key factor that influences the asymptotic distribution's structure, and for values of 'b' greater than two, the structure can be understood through a mixture of power laws, while for values less than two, it can be understood through a mixture of laws that exhibit a different type of behavior, often referred to as the 'Larkin regime'. Furthermore, it is shown that the Larkin regime can be further divided into two sub-regimes, namely the 'large deviations regime' for values of 'b' greater than one and the 'Larkin regime' for values less than one. Lastly, a more general result is proven, which provides an understanding of the asymptotic distribution under the condition of stationary increments with zero mean, and it is demonstrated that this distribution consists of a product of two independent components, one of which is responsible for the asymptotic behavior and can be represented by the cumulative distribution function of the generalized gamma distribution, and the other of which represents the asymptotic behavior in the tail and can be represented by the cumulative distribution function of the generalized inverse Weibull distribution. All of these results can be applied to a broad class of random walk models, including self-similar processes, such as fractional Brownian motion and its relatives, and multi-fractional Brownian motion. Moreover, the work also offers an analytical approach to assessing the performance of model selection procedures in statistics. The Hamiltonian path index of a graph H is the total number of Hamiltonian paths within H. This research aims to extend an investigation initially conducted by Fiyaklo and Semerci in 2019, which focused on the hamiltonian path index of cubic graphs. This research presents a new verification approach for Michelson programs used in Tezos, an open-source platform for blockchain-based smart contracts. A specialized tool, called HELMHOLTZ, leverages a combination of static and dynamic verification methods to complement an existing SMT-based approach, especially for verifying array and map applications within Michelson programs. Through a set of predefined templates and counterexamples, HELMHOLTZ can effectively test the validity of certain program operations, such as function arguments, and even develop tailored queries for static analysis purposes. By integrating these techniques, we demonstrate a significant improvement in the verification of Michelson programs, particularly for programs involving arrays and maps, where the success rate is doubled when compared to an existing method based on SMT solvers. Furthermore, we show that HELMHOLTZ's approach can also be employed to verify programs involving mutable reference cells. A user-friendly web interface, developed using a reactive web framework, allows users to paste and verify their own Michelson programs using HELMHOLTZ, in addition to exploring various program configurations. A set of programs, both correct and incorrect, serves as examples for demonstrating HELMHOLTZ's capabilities and verification processes. The Michelson Verification Toolkit, which incorporates HELMHOLTZ, is now available at https://michelson.verifypw.io/, providing a publicly accessible environment where users can experiment with the verification of their own Michelson programs. This research is part of an ongoing effort to establish a comprehensive verification framework for the Michelson programming language. By combining static and dynamic verification methods, we aim to tackle the challenges associated with verifying smart contracts, particularly those related to the lack of type systems and garbage collection in Michelson programs. Although contract developers can program directly on the Tezos network, using a compiler for Michelson, researchers like ourselves can compile the same contracts and send them to the network for verification and eventual deployment. Consequently, we believe that verifying Michelson programs through a combination of static and dynamic verification methods can benefit the Tezos community by contributing to the reliability of smart contracts and ensuring the security of the Tezos network. Moreover, our verification approach is designed to be adaptable for use with other programming languages and contexts where counterexample-driven validation can be applied. Despite GCNs being the current leading approach, research into understanding the fundamental connections between GCNs and traditional neural networks, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks, can provide valuable insights and simplify the implementation of novel graph neural networks. This work provides a geometric interpretation of GCNs, CNNs, and fully connected Neural Networks on their respective input domains, visualizing them as projections of high-dimensional data onto lower-dimensional spaces and exhibiting their relationships through combinations of linear transformations and point projections. By leveraging this geometric interpretation, we are able to introduce a suite of novel graph neural networks, combining the principles of CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks, and demonstrate their effectiveness through comprehensive evaluations on multiple datasets for both node classification and graph classification tasks. The code for these models has been made publicly available. As a result of this research, graph neural networks can now be developed with existing neural network components in mind, offering a range of possibilities for the creation of more innovative graph neural networks. As a consequence, there is a pressing need to develop techniques that can convert specs into executable code, thereby tightening the link between specifications and implementations. This paper delves into the advantages that can be achieved by converting specifications from traditional pseudocodes to logical pseudocodes, which offer a more precise representation that can be executed with greater safety and accuracy. To realize this benefit, we propose a method that leverages learning algorithms to bridge the gap between these two forms, thereby enabling the translation of safe and correct protocols into efficient code. Additionally, we provide explicit formulas for calculating the numbers of nontransitive n-tuples consisting of repeated and distinct elements. The concept of deformed halo structures, particularly in rotating nuclei like Lead-205, has sparked intense debate in nuclear physics. To shed light on this debate, our research employs a microscopic approach using the angular momentum projection method onto deformed states. Our findings reveal that rotating nuclei can exhibit halo characteristics without shifting to spherical shapes, and involve complex configurations of rotational states within their ground states. These results lead to modified density distributions in rotating nuclei, and their implications are explored through the calculation of electric dipole form factors. Our study demonstrates the crucial role of factoring in rotating nuclei's deformed shapes, and highlights the necessity of considering multiple angular momentum projections for an accurate understanding of such nuclei. Furthermore, our results suggest that rotating nuclei like Lead-205 may exhibit two-neutron halo properties, and that the angular momentum projection method can be utilized to investigate the configurations of rotating nuclei's ground states. Additionally, our study proposes the use of monopole strength as a new tool for distinguishing between spherical and deformed shapes in rotating nuclei. By applying this approach to a range of two-neutron halo nuclei, including Lead-205, Lead-208, Carbon-17, Oxygen-17, Magnesium-24, Sulfur-32, and Radium-212, our research provides a framework for re-examining the very concept of rotating deformed halo nuclei.

Generalized balanced sampling (GBS) is an adaptable variation of the balanced sampling (BS) approach. A novel algorithm has been developed to efficiently identify a balanced sample from a large data set. The existing BS algorithm is typically implemented using a systematic search method, which ensures that the sample remains balanced as it is modified. However, this approach is highly time-consuming and becomes unfeasible for large data sets. The newly devised algorithm reduces the time required to find a GBS and generates samples for various measures such as the mean, ratio, and frequency. The algorithm achieves this by modifying the original BS method, which selects a balanced sample based on specific characteristics, such as mean or ratio values. Instead of searching for samples that match these characteristics, the new algorithm calculates the required sample size and finds the most efficient subset. The algorithm has a linear complexity and outperforms the existing BS algorithm by reducing the time required from O(n^2) to O(n). The new algorithm can handle data sets with continuous or categorical characteristics and can be applied to complex measures that combine multiple variables. This paper examines the concept of invariance in fractional order systems and establishes the requirements for linear subspaces to remain unaffected under the systems' dynamics. We demonstrate that the condition of invariance depends on the systems' dynamics and that this condition can be met with control inputs. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for the subspace to become invariant in the absence of external forces. Additionally, we differentiate between two types of invariance, namely, reachability invariance and stability invariance, and explore their distinct properties. We also present an example involving a fractional order Ricker model to illustrate the concept of invariance and its connection to the system's dynamics. We conclude the paper by highlighting the significance of invariance in fractional order systems and propose potential areas for further research in this field. Lastly, we provide a framework for extending the concept of invariance to multiple fractional order systems and present computational tools for analyzing invariance in such systems. These tools are made available online as a part of the MatConFlex matrix manipulation software. We also outline the advantages of utilizing MatConFlex over other matrix computation software. We end by highlighting the potential applications of invariance analysis in various scientific disciplines, such as ecology, biology, and control theory. We also discuss the potential for further research in this field, particularly in relation to systems with time-varying parameters and multiple fractional order systems with interaction between them. We conclude by expressing our research in relation to other works in this field and propose new directions for research in this area. We are the first to introduce the concept of invariance in this context and have developed all necessary theoretical and computational frameworks to that end. We hope that our work will serve as a foundation for researchers to explore the concept of invariance in multiple fractional order systems and encourage them to consider our proposed framework as a starting point for their research. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this software through our analysis of the Ricker model. Annotating large sets of text documents for machine learning is a time-consuming process, often requiring a team to manually label data across multiple tasks. Even with a large and motivated team, the annotation process can become a bottleneck when building highly accurate NLP models. To speed up the process, we've developed a method to automate annotations by training models that can generate high-quality, task-relevant text based on given prompts. By leveraging the findings of previous studies on prompt-based models and data augmentation, we've identified several key factors that contribute to the success of annotation-free models or models that can generate accurate annotations. However, these models still fall short in certain scenarios, especially when they involve less common NLP tasks or demand greater precision. To bridge this gap, we suggest a hybrid approach that combines model-based generation with human review and editing. Through experimentation on multiple tasks and datasets, we've seen significant improvements in model performance, with some results showing gains of up to 20 points in F1 score when human editors are involved. The hybrid approach also enables faster development cycles, as models can be fine-tuned more quickly and with greater effectiveness. By automating the annotation process in part, we've been able to reduce the overall cost per annotation by a factor of five. In addition, we've introduced a new framework called Bidirectional Prompt Learning that enables models to generate annotations and learn from those generated texts at the same time. This has led to greater accuracy and efficiency. We've made our code and models available publicly, hoping that it will inspire further innovation in the field. This is a fundamental problem that needs to be addressed before NLP models can be widely adopted, and we're excited to contribute our findings to the ongoing pursuit of this goal. This study examines how the atmosphere of planets located at a moderate distance from their stars is affected by their host star's properties, specifically metal content, which we previously found to have a significant impact. We are investigating the atmospheres of six planets in the M-dwarf systems K2-25d, K2-19c, K2-11b, K2-9b, K2-2b, and K2-18b with temperatures between 400K to 1000K. Using a grid of models, we analyzed how the composition of these planets' atmospheres is affected by their cooling history, atmospheric loss, and primordial composition, and then compared this to spectroscopic observations. For the hotter planets, we found that a gas-rich atmosphere results from a sustained volcanic gas supply, and this leads to an envelope that is enveloped by a cooler, more gas-poor outer layer. On the other hand, the temperate planets' atmospheres hold substantial metals and volatiles, and we can predict abundance levels of various gases based on their eccentricities and stellar environments. Specifically, we can predict abundance levels of CO, CO2, and NH3, and also determine how these planets lose mass through atmospheric entry or a mass-loss cycle induced by massive storms. Furthermore, this analysis also highlights the significance of accurately determining the stellar metal content of these systems, and also highlights potential biases in planetary selection based on stellar parameters. Lastly, this study implies that a correlation exists between the metal content of the host star and the volatility content of the planet's atmosphere, and this correlation holds true for both the inner and outer planets. Our study offers an examination of the zero-energy peak and end-anomaly in Majorana nanowires, undeterred by non-Majorana influences, at both zero and finite temperatures. A self-consistent solution to the BTE and LE are employed to investigate the behavior of proximity-induced levels and charge distribution within the device, even in presence of charge instability, by utilizing a 1D numerical model. The model incorporates both spin-momentum locked propagation and interaction with the terminals, thereby enabling a comprehensive investigation of the end-anomaly. Our findings reveal that although the zero-energy peak is slightly modified by non-Majorana effects, they do not substantially impact its overall characterization. Furthermore, the peak remains relatively unchanged down to 0.1 Kelvin, but reduces in amplitude with increasing temperature. Conversely, the end-anomaly exhibits a more intricate temperature dependence, displaying an unusual behavior at 0.1 Kelvin but returning to its zero-energy form at higher temperatures. The model also illustrates how charge instability is handled within this framework. Additionally, our results demonstrate that even without accounting for back-scattering, the end-anomaly can arise due to proximity-induced levels at zero temperature. However, this phenomenon disappears at finite temperatures due to the reduction in level splitting. The study provides new insights necessary for correctly interpreting experimental data related to Majorana modes. Moreover, the zero-energy peak and end-anomaly can serve as a crucial probe for distinguishing between Majorana and non-Majorana modes. The work also highlights the importance of temperature in identifying these exotic modes. The proposed theoretical model can be experimentally verified and refined through ABER and LE measurements, ultimately leading to a better understanding of Majorana modes in nanowires. Highway maintenance agencies face significant challenges in efficiently managing road inspection tasks.  To address this issue, a system called RoadAtlas was developed as part of a broader research initiative.  This system includes an advanced mobile data collection platform and an optimized route-planning tool.  By providing real-time traffic and maintenance data, evaluating route quality, and simulating data collection processes, RoadAtlas can pinpoint optimal inspection paths.  In experiments conducted with real-world data from the California Department of Transportation, RoadAtlas demonstrated a notable increase in overall inspection efficiency.  Compared to traditional methods, this system yielded a 25% reduction in total distance traveled and a 45% decrease in inactive driving time.  Furthermore, REAL-Time traffic data helped inspectors complete their tasks 15% faster on average.  A comparative analysis of different route quality metrics also highlighted the performance differences between data collection paths.  To facilitate replication and advancement of this research, the RoadAtlas platform is now available as an open-source tool.  This includes the mobile data collection application and the route quality assessment framework.  Future developments aimed at enhancing the system's functionality and validity are also being considered.  As a result, this system serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners alike who aim to improve the effectiveness of road inspection processes.  This paper provides an overview of the RoadAtlas platform, detailing its components and showcasing its capabilities through a series of experiments conducted with real-world data from the California Department of Transportation.  The associated data and software are available at https://roadatlas.berkeley.edu/.  This work has been presented in extracted form at the 2021 IEEE Intelligent Transportation Systems Magazine.  A more comprehensive report detailing the methods used can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07818. As a result, the LGCN is capable of representing large-scale hyperbolic graphs more accurately, and significantly outperforms existing HGCN methods in terms of node classification and graph classification tasks. This study focuses on enhancing stability in inverse problems for partial differential equations by establishing an observability inequality with a boundary control. Specifically, it investigates the inverse problem of identifying an initial condition and a nonlinear surface within an incompressible Navier-Stokes equation, where the nonlinear surface affects turbulence and mixing. The research establishes a regularity inequality, known as the observability inequality, which guarantees that small norms on the boundary measurements $y$ can restrict the size of the initial conditions $(v_0,u_0)$ in a Hilbert space. This type of inequality has a significant impact on the stability of inverse problems and is a crucial component in the construction of continuous right-hand sides for an operator involving the n-dimensional Navier-Stokes equation. Building upon this inequality, we demonstrate that a bounded set in the initial conditions can further reduce the time $T$ within a certain condition. Furthermore, this reduced time $T$ results in a continuous right-hand side within the negative Sobolev space. This research also investigates the feasibility of constructing a boundary control to recover both the initial conditions and the nonlinear surface within the Navier-Stokes equation. Combining the observability inequality with a direct operator technique, we establish a stability inequality that restricts the size of the nonlinear surface $S$ under boundary measurements $y$. This leads to the feasibility of constructing a continuous right-hand side for an operator involving the Navier-Stokes equation with a nonlinear boundary condition. Consequently, this research provides a stability inequality that facilitates the recovery of both the initial conditions and the nonlinear surface within the Navier-Stokes equation using boundary control. Additionally, this method results in a continuous right-hand side within the negative Sobolev space, where the nonlinear surface plays a significant role in turbulence and mixing. Notably, this research focuses exclusively on the fractional Navier-Stokes equation. The method proposed here opens up avenues for further investigation into other partial differential equations, including the non-Navier-Stokes equation. It is anticipated that this study will contribute to a better comprehension of the feasibility of constructing continuous right-hand sides for operators involving the Navier-Stokes equation and, more broadly, the role of nonlinear surfaces in turbulence and mixing. It is also hoped that this research will provide a foundation for exploring related problems in fractional differential equations and other partial differential equations. The transformation allows for a significant increase in mesh refinement, thereby enabling accurate solutions to acoustic scattering problems involving sharp edges and corners. The IFEM method is comparable to the Nystrom method in terms of computational cost and offers a more manageable alternative to the direct application of the boundary integral equation. The implementation of IFEM involves transformation-based mesh refinement, non-orthogonal element matrices, and a collocation approach. This method has been successfully applied to solve a range of eigenvalue problems and a fixed-energy problem within the context of acoustic scattering. The results obtained through the IFEM approach have been compared with those of the Nystrom method and Mie series expansions, demonstrating the method's effectiveness and efficiency. The success of the IFEM approach suggests that this method has the potential to be an valuable tool for tackling the challenges posed by high-frequency problems in acoustic scattering. Building upon the existing framework for spin-lattice tensor products, we develop a suitable method to compute the scalar products of integrable higher-spin XXZ chains. This method involves a specific combination of semi-local algebraic and diagonalization techniques. By utilizing the semi-local algebraic method, we obtain the semi-local density matrices for the two-point correlation functions, which we then diagonalize to obtain the form factors. We demonstrate that our approach yields consistent results with previous studies for both finite and infinite chains. We also introduce a novel graphical representation for the semi-local density matrices and form factors, which we visualize for various spin values and chain lengths. Through this representation, we are able to identify distinct patterns and limitations for the form factors, which we further explore through our diagonalization method. Our study provides a comprehensive computational framework for the scalar products and form factors of these chains, enabling us to gain deeper understanding of the underlying physics. As a result, we are able to extract various spin-lattice coefficients that describe the correlations within the chain. These coefficients are crucial for describing the magnetic properties of these systems, especially in the low-spin and low-chain-length regimes. Our study offers a crucial step in developing a systematic series expansion for the density matrix and two-point correlation functions of these integrable systems. We anticipate that our computational framework will prove valuable in enhancing the understanding of finite-size phenomena in these integrable systems. As such, we make our Python code publicly available for the benefit of the scientific community.
